title: Developing acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties to expand faba bean adaption.
description:
Faba bean production in Australia is constrained by soil acidity, particularly in Western Australia, South Australia, southern New South Wales and parts of Victoria, where acidic soils reduce root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop vigour and grain yield. Soil acidity also limits the expansion of faba bean into otherwise suitable production environments. While liming remains an important soil management practice, sub-surface acidity is often difficult, slow and costly to remediate, creating a need for complementary genetic solutions that improve crop performance and profitability on affected soils.
Recent GRDC investments have successfully delivered acid-tolerant rhizobia for faba bean, improving nodulation and nitrogen fixation under low pH conditions. However, the effectiveness of these inoculants depends on successful plant-rhizobia interactions, and current elite faba bean germplasm remains poorly adapted to acid soils (pH (CaCl2) <5.0). Developing acid-soil-tolerant varieties is therefore essential to fully realise the benefits of improved rhizobia strains and maximise productivity in acidic soil environments.
This four-year investment will accelerate the development of acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties by delivering the germplasm, genetic knowledge and breeding tools required to support long-term genetic improvement. The investment will identify and validate novel sources of acid soil tolerance from Australian and international germplasm, improve understanding of the physiological, biochemical and genetic mechanisms underpinning tolerance, and translate these discoveries into practical breeding outcomes for Australian faba bean breeding programs. Controlled-environment screening, field-based validation and modern genomic approaches will identify and characterise traits associated with improved performance on acidic soils, including traits linked to root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop establishment and yield. Activities should address both surface and sub-surface soil acidity and generate robust, field-relevant data to support breeding and selection decisions across target production environments.
A key component of the investment will be the development of validated high-throughput phenotyping methods, screening protocols and molecular markers that enable efficient selection for acid soil tolerance. These tools will support more rapid and cost-effective identification and deployment of favourable alleles within breeding pipelines, accelerating genetic gain for adaptation to acidic soils. Breeder-ready germplasm will incorporate novel acid-soil-tolerance alleles and demonstrating improved performance under acidic soil conditions, with a target yield advantage of at least 10% over benchmark varieties grown on acid soils of pH (CaCl2) below 5.0. Germplasm should be validated across representative production environments and supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and marker datasets to facilitate immediate use in breeding programs.
Strong collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to guide trait prioritisation, validation environments, phenotyping approaches and deployment pathways, ensuring outputs align with breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs.
The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the genetic resources, screening tools and knowledge required to develop future faba bean varieties with improved adaptation to acid soils, enhanced yield stability and increased productivity. These advances will complement existing soil amelioration practices and acid-tolerant rhizobia, support expansion into suitable regions, improve reliability on acid soils and strengthen the competitiveness and sustainability of the Australian faba bean industry.

title: Enhancing faba bean seed colour and seed size uniformity to increase the value of faba beans and reduce risk of classifi
description:
Faba bean is an important Australian pulse crop and export commodity, supplying premium food and feed markets where visual grain quality is a key determinant of market access, classification and value. Buyers place strong emphasis on seed coat colour, colour retention and seed size uniformity, with these traits directly influencing grading outcomes, market acceptance and the price received throughout the value chain. Variability in visual grain quality, together with seed coat darkening during storage and handling, can increase the risk of downgrades, reduce grower returns and weaken Australia’s competitive advantage in premium export markets.
Although visual grain quality is known to have a strong genetic component, the biological, biochemical and environmental factors influencing seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity are not well understood. Australian breeding programs currently have limited access to the genetic resources, molecular markers and high-throughput phenotyping tools needed to efficiently improve these traits. Recent advances in genomics, artificial intelligence, digital imaging and data analytics provide new opportunities to accelerate genetic gain and develop more effective breeding solutions.
This four-year investment will develop the knowledge, genetic resources and breeding-enabling tools required to improve seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity in Australian faba beans. The investment will investigate the genetic, physiological, biochemical and environmental drivers underlying visual grain quality, including the mechanisms responsible for seed coat oxidation and post-harvest darkening. Activities should consider both genetic and non-genetic contributors to trait expression, including the effects of storage conditions, handling practices and environmental influences on grain quality outcomes.
A key component of the investment will be the development and validation of modern phenotyping and analytical tools to enable routine selection for visual grain quality traits. This includes the application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital imaging and high-throughput phenotyping approaches to objectively measure seed coat colour stability, seed size uniformity and other commercially important visual attributes. Identification and incorporation of valuable genetic variation for improved seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity will enable development of breeder-ready germplasm for use in Australian faba bean breeding programs. Germplasm should demonstrate measurable improvements in visual grain quality traits and be supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and validated molecular marker datasets to facilitate rapid integration into breeding pipelines.
Strong and ongoing collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to help guide trait prioritisation, phenotyping methods, validation activities and deployment pathways. This will ensure outputs are aligned with market requirements and breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into crossing blocks, breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs.
The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the germplasm, molecular markers, phenotyping tools and knowledge required to accelerate the development of future faba bean varieties with improved visual grain quality, greater market suitability and reduced risk of classification downgrades. These advances will help maintain existing market premiums, improve storage and marketing flexibility, protect Australia's reputation as a supplier of high-quality faba beans and strengthen the long-term competitiveness and value of the Australian faba bean industry.

title: ACRCP6-Integrated Rust Initiative: Program 3. Integrated Disease Management and Extension
description:
Cereal rust diseases continue to pose a significant and evolving threat to Australian wheat, barley and oat production. Wheat rust alone costs the Australian grains industry $147 million pa when controlled with genetics and current management practices, but predicted losses are close to $1.7 billion pa if no control occurs (Murray and Brennan, 2009). Rust pathogens are highly adaptable and have repeatedly overcome deployed genetic resistance and chemical control options, resulting in yield losses, increased fungicide use and rising production costs for growers. While the Australian Cereal Rust Control Program (ACRCP) has delivered strong outcomes over multiple phases, the increasing complexity of pathogen evolution (E.g. Yr15 virulent pathogen and BGYR pathogen evolution), fungicide sensitivity, loss of access to chemistry risk and climate driven disease pressure requires a more integrated and future focused investment approach.
The next phase will bring these activities together in a coordinated national initiative. It will strengthen rust surveillance, accelerate the development and use of durable genetic resistance, and improve integrated disease management across production systems. Expanding the program beyond wheat to include barley and oats will allow proven approaches and lessons to benefit the broader grains industry.
The Australian Cereal Rust Control Program Phase 6 (ACRCP6) – Integrated Rust Initiative will build on existing capability while addressing gaps in coordination, efficiency and preparedness for emerging rust threats. By supporting more durable crop resistance, responsible fungicide use and better-informed decisions by breeders, advisers and growers, the initiative aims to reduce the long-term cost and impact of cereal rust.
This procurement is specifically for the Integrated Disease Management (IDM) and Extension component of ACRCP6. GRDC is seeking a provider to identify priority rust management gaps, develop and update practical IDM strategies, and translate surveillance, crop resistance, seasonal risk and fungicide stewardship information into timely resources and advice for growers and advisers. The work will support more effective rust management, reduce reliance on reactive fungicide use and improve the grains industry’s long-term resilience.

title: Establishing pigeon pea as a summer pulse crop in the Northern Region
description:
Description:
The northern grains industry is seeking a more reliable summer legume option for hotter, drier farming environments where current commercial options are limited. While mungbean and soybean are well-established in some parts of the northern region, their higher water requirements and sensitivity to heat, seasonal stress and limited stored soil moisture can make them less dependable in lower-rainfall areas. This limits growers’ ability to confidently include a summer legume in rotations, reducing opportunities to improve system diversity, nitrogen inputs and overall farming system resilience.
Pigeon pea has been identified as a potential crop to address this gap. Its drought tolerance, resilience in constrained soils and ability to withstand more extreme seasonal conditions make it a strong candidate for environments where mungbean and soybean are not consistently reliable. Early GRDC-supported work has demonstrated that pigeon pea can be grown successfully across initial target environments in southern Queensland, central Queensland and northern New South Wales, and has helped identify promising genetic material and preliminary management considerations.
This investment will engage a delivery partner to design and deliver a coordinated field trial, extension and industry development program that builds on previous GRDC-supported pigeon pea work. The program will validate key agronomic practices across northern farming environments, generate evidence on yield potential, grain quality and farming system fit, and develop practical management guidance for growers and advisers. The delivery partner will also extend findings through targeted engagement with growers, advisers, industry and supply chain stakeholders, and provide the data and samples needed to support market development, future pre-breeding priorities and minor use permit applications. This investment is intended to be GRDC’s primary mechanism for improving the profitability, industry readiness and adoption of pigeon pea as a viable summer pulse option for the Northern Region.
Outcome:
<span">By 30 September 2030, growers in the target region of south-west and central Qld have the confidence to plant and profitably manage pigeon pea across 30,000ha thereby achieving a minimum viable industry.
Outputs.
Output 1.
Title: Develop tailored agronomic practices to achieve full yield for pigeonpea grown in Queensland in North NSW.
Description:
By October and annually thereafter, the investment will establish field experiments ti validate key agronomic practices tailored to pigeonpea production across Queensland and northern NSW. These practices will build on previous GRDC research and incorporate novel management tactics to better define yield potential across different cropping systems and environments. Experiments will be conducted across the GRDC sub-regions of NE NSW, NW NSW, SE QLD, SW QLD and Central QLD.
Field trials will evaluate the following:
- - Yield potential and ideal growing traits for each region/climate.
- - Agronomic management options e.g. sowing date, sowing configurations, fertiliser application, irrigation, etc.
- - Producing optimal grain standards for end users.
- - Pest management guidelines.
- - Disease critical thresholds.
- - Legacy implication of implementing pigeonpea into a farming systems e.g. nitrogen legacy.
The service provider will be required to work closely with GRDC’s CP&I team through AKC2507-001SAX to ensure project data is available to support minor use permit applications, particularly for desiccation, as well as insect and weed management issues.
The field experiments to develop key agronomic management plans tailored for each sub-region, providing clear guidance for growers to adopt and implement in their cropping systems.
Output 2.
Title: Extension and adoption of best management practices.
Description:
The project will deliver a coordinated extension and adoption pathway annually between 2027 and 2030. The pathway will be developed with early adopter insights and tailored to growers, advisers and supply chain participations across the northern sub-regions. Activities will move beyond field days and publications to maintain grower interest and momentum throughout the project, support peer-to-peer learning, build adviser capability and strengthen broader industry confidence in pigeonpea as a viable summer pulse option.
The activities may include:
- - Technical grower management plans tailored to each sub-region and cropping system.
- - Regional demonstration sites and annual field walks at key experiment locations to sow best management practice under commercial conditions.
- - Peer-to-peer learning activities, including grower case studies, paddock-based discussions, decision-support resources and targeted updates that enable advisers to support adoption.
- - Ongoing communication through GRDC GroundCover, digital media, videos, podcasts, social media and seasonal updates.
- - Engagement with supply chain participants, seed suppliers, marketers and potential end users to build confidence in production, grain quality requirements and market pathways.
- - Broader industry engagement with relevant grower groups, agribusiness networks and partner organisations to support coordinated adoption and reduce the risk of fragmented industry development.
Output 3.
Title: Gather supporting information for market requirement and pre-breeding priorities.
Description:
By June 2030, the investment will generate and apply key data and project findings to inform grain industry requirements and priorities future pre-breeding needs for pigeonpea. Building on previous desktop studies and exploratory work, the project will validate Australia’s capacity to produce commercial quantities of pigeonpea for human consumption and feedstock markets.
The project will work with industry participants to provide the samples, data and evidence required to inform grain quality standards. MRLs and priority pre-breeding targets for future investments.

title: Barley Net Blotch Initiative (BNBI) Program 2 – Host and pathogen genetics
description:
Net blotches pose an escalating and urgent threat to Australian barley, costing the industry an estimated $122 million each year through disease-related yield losses, downgraded grain quality, and higher fungicide management costs. Widespread planting of susceptible varieties, the practice of growing barley on barley, and an over-reliance on fungicides with a singular mode of action are driving net blotch pathogens to evolve and spread faster than current surveillance, varietal resistance breeding, management and extension efforts can respond.
This investment seeks to help Australian barley growers keep ahead of a threat that is moving faster than current tools can handle. It will be delivered through a five-year, nationally focused Barley Net Blotch Initiative (BNBI) comprising three interlinked programs supported by a dedicated coordinator:
? Program 1 - Pathogen surveillance, monitoring, and screening
? Program 2- Host and pathogen genetics
? Program 3 - Integrated disease management and extension
? Program C - Coordination and capacity development
GRDC is seeking a capable partner to deliver BNBI Program 2 that will fast-track delivery of high levels of durable host resistance in well-adapted backgrounds supported by breeder-deployable validated markers, characterised resistance sources, insights and capability from foundational and expanded pathogenic genomics research, a new durability risk-assessment framework, and a feasibility assessment of genome-editing capability.

title: Optimising agronomy of irrigated crops to enhance profit per megalitre of water
description:
The work will synthesise evidence from previous GRDC irrigated agriculture investments and assess priority opportunities to improve profitability from irrigated cropping systems, with a focus on maximising profit per megalitre of irrigation water rather than yield or water-use efficiency alone.
The analysis must consider the agronomic and economic drivers that influence irrigated crop decisions, including water availability, water price, input costs, seasonal conditions, crop potential, crop end use, rotations, and whole-farm water allocation. It must also assess how irrigation delivery systems and practices, including surface or furrow and pressurised sprinkler systems, interact with soil physical constraints and crop management factors to influence crop performance, input efficiency and profit per megalitre. For this procurement, irrigated crops primarily refers to grain crops within GRDC’s remit. The analysis should also consider how these crops compete with, complement or interact with other irrigated enterprises, including rice, cotton, forages and mixed farming systems, where relevant to whole-farm water allocation and opportunity costs.
The successful tenderer will be required to review existing irrigation and crop decision-support tools, identify whether they are meeting grower needs, and assess whether practical economic tools or decision frameworks are required to support more confident and timely irrigation research investment decisions across winter and summer cropping scenarios.
The final output will be a clear, evidence-based report that identifies priority research gaps, high-leverage agronomic opportunities, and practical recommendations to guide future GRDC investment in irrigated agronomy at national and regional scales.

title: Understanding barriers and enablers to IPM adoption in Australian grains
description:
Australian grain growers are managing pests in an increasingly complex and constrained environment. Key challenges include increasing insecticide resistance, changing access to crop protection products, regulatory and market pressures, emerging and episodic pest threats, and the need to protect beneficial insects and biological control services while preserving the effectiveness of available chemistry.
GRDC has previously invested in integrated pest management (IPM) adoption, extension and research into the factors that influence practice change across a range of grain-growing regions and pest systems. This provides an important foundation, but much of the earlier adoption work was undertaken before the current level of pressure from insecticide resistance and chemical access constraints, and before more recent changes in how growers and advisers access information and make pest-management decisions.
GRDC is seeking a suitably qualified provider or multidisciplinary team to undertake an independent opportunity analysis examining the barriers, enablers and pathways influencing practical IPM adoption in Australian grain systems. The analysis will draw on existing evidence, current and previous GRDC and industry investments, available tools and resources, relevant experience from other agricultural industries and international cropping systems, and the perspectives of growers, advisers, researchers, extension and adoption practitioners, and other relevant stakeholders.
The work must consider the technical, behavioural, advisory, commercial and broader system-level factors influencing grower and adviser practice change. It must establish a contemporary understanding of current IPM adoption capability, barriers and enabling conditions; assess what has changed since previous IPM adoption and extension investments; and identify the audiences, circumstances and delivery approaches where future effort is most likely to improve practical adoption outcomes.
GRDC requires practical, evidence-based and decision-ready recommendations to guide the design of future research, development, extension and adoption investments in IPM. The work is intended to focus on adoption and practice-change pathways rather than undertake a detailed technical review of individual pests or pest-management tactics. Where technical limitations are affecting adoption, these should be identified as matters that may require further research and development.

title: Grain Automate Open Innovation Call
description:
Grain Automate is a national research, development and extension initiative of the Grains Research and Development Corporation. It seeks to accelerate the development, validation and adoption of machine automation, autonomy and intelligent systems, across a range of form factors, including machinery, implements, UAVs and digital systems, that deliver measurable value to Australian grain growers. The initiative is largely focused within the farm gate, while recognising relevant connections with logistics, suppliers and post-farm-gate systems.
The initiative complements existing investment in precision agriculture, digital agronomy and advanced analytics. It recognises that grower value will be created through a combination of industry readiness, targeted technology development, integration across physical and digital systems, and step-change improvements in precision. This call builds on the approach of the Grain Automate Program.

title: Operational Energy Transitions Defence Research Centre Lead Partner
description:
The Commonwealth is undertaking two separate but related approaches to market (ATM) in parallel to support the establishment of the OET DRC and the delivery of its Inaugural Research Projects (IRPs). The processes being undertaken include:
a. ATM ID 13016 Lead Partner Request For Tender (RFT) (this RFT): to engage a supplier as a Lead Partner to provide research leadership and expertise at the program and project level for the OET DRC; and
b. ATM ID 13457 Contributing Partner Request For Information (RFI) (separate process): to engage with the market for the purposes of:
(i) understanding market capability and potential suppliers that align with, and have interest in, research related to the OET DRC; and
(ii) informing the development and conduct of this Lead Partner RFT as well as future procurement processes.
The Contributing Partner RFI:
a. is separate from, does not form part of, this RFT; and
b. is governed by its own separate process. Further details on the Contributing Partner ATM can be found on AusTender.
You are invited to submit a tender in response to Request for Tender (RFT) 13016 to provide research leadership and management services for the Operational Energy Transitions Defence Research Centre (OET DRC).
Defence Innovation, Science and Technology Strategy 2026 (DISTS 26) calls for Defence to progress the formation of DRCs in partnership with universities and industry to focus on enduring and complex IS&T priorities that require interdisciplinary teams.
The OET DRC is a response to a fundamental shift in the role of energy within Defence capability and operations. It is intended to provide Defence with a scalable and enduring mechanism to shape the Defence energy landscape and deliver operationally relevant, deployable energy solutions that support the future Integrated Force
The OET DRC will operate as a problem-led, outcome-focused enterprise, integrating Defence, academia, industry and international partners into a coherent, mission-driven effort. Its role is not to conduct isolated, exploratory or basic research, but to accelerate the adoption, integration, and transition of energy technologies into deployable Defence capability, particularly where conventional market or program mechanisms are insufficient.

description:
Training Authority Maritime Warfare (TA-MW) is the principal warfare training authority of the Royal Australian Navy (RAN). TAMW comprises several schools which provide warfare training for all rank levels from Seaman to Captain via a wide variety of courses ranging from one week to one year. These courses vary from basic operator training to advanced warfare training (procedural and tactical).
The Royal Australian Navy School of Survivability and Ship's Safety South (RAN SSSS-South) is one of three Damage Control Schools within the Royal Australian Navy (RAN) that sits under TA-MW. RAN SSSS-South delivers damage control and survivability training to personnel of all ranks, from Seaman through to Captain, across a wide range of short-duration courses. The services required for RAN SSSS South Sustainment Support Contract involves establishing, implementing, and conducting sound engineering maintenance practices through the application of Planned Maintenance (PM) and Reliability-Centered Maintenance (RCM) methodologies for key training aids located at Royal Australian Navy School of Survivability and Ship's Safety South (RAN SSSS-S), HMAS Cerberus.

title: Private Hospital Services
description:
DVA is seeking the provision of Private Hospital services for Entitled Persons by publishing this Invitation to Provide Private Hospital Services to the Veteran Community.
DVA serves Australia’s veteran community, through the provision of programmes of care, compensation and commemoration.
DVA’s aim is to secure high quality private hospital care for Entitled Persons delivered for a fair price, at the most convenient locations for Entitled Persons. As the veteran community ages, their capacity to access a wider range of care appropriate to their needs is increasingly important. Managing emerging and different needs of contemporary veterans is also a priority. DVA also aims to continually improve the quality and safety of services, and the health outcomes for DVA clients, through the purchase of evidence-based treatment services.
DVA’s New Approach to Contracting for Private Hospital Services
In the past DVA contracted with Private Hospitals for services to Entitled Persons through a Request for Tenders (RFT).
The current process that DVA is engaging in with Private Hospital providers is not an RFT.
DVA has introduced new arrangements for providers to contract with DVA. This is a simplified contracting model that DVA is using to facilitate engagement with suitably qualified providers.
A summary of the key features of the new arrangements are:
maximising the numbers of participating providers to achieve wide access to private hospitals services for the veteran community;
there is no competition, all qualified providers can participate;
while providers are required to submit the fee tables, there is no requirement for tender submission or evaluation of tenders;
providers self-certify their compliance with DVA’s terms and conditions of the Hospital Services Agreement;
providers can enter into the Hospital Services Agreement at any time and the Hospital Services Agreement will continue until DVA ends the arrangements or the Contracting Entity exits the arrangements with DVA; and
negotiation only on fees to ensure value for money.

title: Operational Energy Transitions Defence Research Centre Contributing Partner RFI
description:
The OET DRC is being developed in response to a fundamental shift in the role of energy within Defence capability and operations. Energy is no longer a background enabler, but a central determinant of operational effectiveness, underpinning operational tempo, persistence, survivability, and freedom of action in increasingly contested and degraded environments.
To support the establishment of the OET DRC and the delivery of its Inaugural Research Projects (IRPs), the Commonwealth is undertaking two separate but related processes in parallel as follows:
1. ATM ID 13016 Lead Partner Request For Tender (RFT) (separate process): to engage a supplier as a Lead Partner to provide research leadership and expertise at the program and project level for the OET DRC; and
2. ATM ID 13457 Contributing Partner Request For Information (RFI) (this RFI): to engage with the market for the purposes of:
- understanding market capability and potential suppliers that align with, and have interest in, research related to the OET DRC Themes; and
- informing the development and conduct of other procurement processes (including future procurement processes).
This RFI is separate from the Lead Partner RFT process. Further information regarding the Lead Partner RFT can be found on AusTender under ATM ID 13016.
The OET DRC will initially address the following five areas (OET DRC Themes):
1. Dispersed Energy Access at the Tactical Edge
2. Sustainment Under Contested Conditions
3. Resilient and Scalable Forward Energy Systems
4. Enabling Next-Generation High-Power and High-Consumption Capabilities
5. Extended Endurance and Reduced Logistic Dependence
Defence’s overall objective is to support innovative, low Technology Readiness Level research that advances new knowledge, develops emerging concepts or prototypes and has the potential to contribute to future capability outcomes associated with the OET DRC Themes.
This RFI invites entities interested in the OET DRC Themes to provide a response that outlines their research expertise, capability and facilities. Respondents are also invited to put forward unique or novel research and technology approaches to enable practical solutions under the OET DRC Themes.

The Department of Home Affairs is seeking to re-establish the Job Roles Assessment and Services (JRAS) Panel through an open tender process. The new panel will replace the existing JRAS Panel arrangement, which is due to expire in 2027.
The Department requires access to suitably qualified and experienced providers to deliver a range of health-related assessment and associated services that support the health, wellbeing and fitness of the Home Affairs Portfolio workforce.
These services assist the Department in assessing the suitability of candidates for particular roles and in ensuring existing workers continue to meet the health, fitness and wellbeing requirements of their roles.
The procurement will seek providers capable of delivering services across one or more of the following Service Capabilities:
- Medical and Fitness Assessments, including medical assessments and fitness testing.
- Psychological and Psychometric Assessments.
- Exposure to Abhorrent, Violent or Objectionable Materials Services, including wellbeing check programs, general monitoring services and specialist monitoring services.
- Vaccinations and Communicable Disease Testing, including services to mitigate occupational infectious disease risks.
The resulting panel will be established under a Deed of Standing Offer and is intended to provide the Department with a flexible arrangement through which services can be procured as required. Individual requirements will be engaged through Work Orders established under the panel arrangement. The procurement is being led by the Department of Home Affairs and will support the broader Home Affairs Portfolio, including the Australian Border Force (ABF). The resulting panel will also be available for use by other Commonwealth agencies.

title: EOI - Supply of Direct Drive Chiller
description:
The Australian Synchrotron (AS) is a world-class research facility operated by the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO) at Clayton, Victoria. The facility operates continuously and relies on a central refrigeration system to provide chilled water for critical facility heat loads, including low-conductivity water (LCW) cooling and HVAC systems.
Chiller 1 is one of four chillers serving the primary cooling circuit. It is approximately 22 years old, has accumulated significant run hours and has reached end of life, with spare parts no longer readily available. Replacement is required to restore reliable N+1 cooling redundancy and reduce the risk of loss of critical cooling capacity.
The existing system supplies chilled water at approximately 6°C, with return water at approximately 10°C. The condenser water circuit typically enters the chiller at approximately 20°C and leaves at approximately 23°C for heat rejection through the cooling towers.
buyer: Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation

title: Notice of RFT - Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel of Outreach Program Counsellors for the
description:
This is a pre-release notice to provide advance notification of a proposed RFT for the Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel.
Please note, eligibility, application requirements, assessment processes, and contractual arrangements will be set out in the forthcoming RFT. No evaluation criteria, scoring methodology, or commercial terms are being released at this stage. The Department reserves the right to modify or cancel the proposed RFT at its discretion.
Background on Open Arms
Open Arms is Australia’s national accredited provider of mental health and wellbeing services for veterans and the families of veterans.
Open Arms provides mental health counselling, relationship counselling, peer support services, and group programs for people with Australian Defence Force (ADF) service (current and former serving members) and their immediate families.
Open Arms provides free and confidential counselling through a national network of multidisciplinary mental health professionals, delivered in dedicated Open Arms centres by the DVA’s staff, or through the Panel; being a network of accredited mental health clinicians, engaged to support the delivery of services on behalf of Open Arms across Australia through the Outreach Program.
Open Arms can provide counselling, care coordination and peer support services to veterans and the families of veterans within an episode of care model, where clients engage with our services for goal directed interventions for a defined period.
Open Arms aims to provide timely access to appropriate services and care, based on a comprehensive holistic assessment and integrated care pathways to meet client needs and support recovery. This includes working in partnership with health systems, including primary health, as well as other community agencies to ensure comprehensive support for our clients.
Background on the Panel and Outreach Program
Open Arms’ Model of Care provides the organisational framework that underpins the delivery of all Outreach Program services. It guides how we support veterans and the families of veterans through trauma-informed, military-aware, recovery-oriented care, while ensuring consistent clinical governance, quality service delivery and positive client outcomes. In 2024 the Panel was established through which Outreach Providers provide Open Arms services to clients. The Panel is the mechanism for Open Arms to engage with Outreach Providers to ensure the highest level of support can be delivered to clients. Only organisations or individuals appointed to the Panel can provide Open Arms Outreach Program Counselling Services.
The categories of services that are delivered through the Panel include:
Outreach Program Counsellors (OPCs), who provide individual, couples, or family counselling
Group Program Facilitators (GPFs), who facilitate evidence-informed, military-aware group programs that strengthen resilience, build practical skills, and promote wellbeing
Clinical Supervisors, who provide professional supervision to Open Arms’ staff.
Outreach Providers on the Panel can provide one, two or all three service streams, depending on their qualifications, experience and the services they are approved to deliver.
Go to the Open Arms website for further information:
https://www.openarms.gov.au/about/open-arms-outreach-program
Expansion of definition of OPC
In 2025 the Veterans’ Entitlements (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025 and the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025), were enacted which amended the MRCA Treatment Principles (No. MRCC 53/2013) and the Treatment Principles (Instrument 2013 No. R52) – (collectively the Treatment Principles) – to expand the types of professions who can provide Outreach Program Counselling as an Outreach Program Counsellor (OPC). Now that occupational therapists, registered nurses, social workers (general) and counsellors are recognised as additional profession types eligible to apply to become a provider, the Department wishes to update the Panel accordingly through the proposed RFT.
The Department is therefore looking to procure Outreach Providers from the following eligible professions:
a person who is registered with AHPRA as a psychologist;
a person who is registered with AHPRA as an occupational therapist;
a person who is registered with AHPRA as a registered nurse;
a person who is eligible for membership with the Australian Association of Social Workers;
or
a person who is registered:
as a registered clinical counsellor with the Psychotherapy and Counselling Federation of Australia;
as a counsellor at registration category Level 3 or Level 4 with the Australian Counselling Association Limited.
The Department is currently planning to release the RFT to market through publication on AusTender in September 2026, however this timeframe may be subject to change.
Please note that this is not an RFT and does not commit the Department to proceed. The Close Date and Time stated in this notice relates to this pre-release notice only and does not reflect the proposed RFT commencement and closing dates for potential tenderers to lodge their submissions. The RFT, where undertaken, will be published on AusTender and will include the Closing Date and Time for lodgement of submissions.

title: Navy Way Point Leadership Program
description:
Navy Training Authority Initial Training Leadership and Management (TA-ITLM) requires a suitably qualified Supplier to develop and deliver the Navy Way Point program. The program is designed to complement the current Navy Senior Leadership Program (NSLP) and other existing career professional development offerings.
In order to provide a more career-focused professional development opportunity for Captains, particularly those who are new to the Canberra environment, Navy is seeking a reality-based program with a focus on participant interaction, containing practical exercises based on real world scenarios.
The aim of the Way Point Program is to develop the ability of selected senior officers to comprehend the strategic environment and to provide influential, Joint and Whole of Australian Government (WoAG) options that support Government strategic objectives. The course should develop participants' strategic comprehension, thinking and communication skills, and the behaviours and attitudes needed to be effective as a commander or senior staff officer in a Joint, Defence and WoAG team.
The program should include a broad range of highly experienced presenters from across the national security spectrum, with the intent to provide officers new to the Canberra environment, with the skills and confidence operating with influence in Joint, Defence, WoAG and international environments.
Each Navy Way Point program shall be five (5) days in length for up to 24 participants. Taking place in Canberra once per calendar year, with delivery in Q2 (April-June).

title: Call for Expressions of Interest: System Restart Service (SWIS-wide)
description:
AEMO is seeking Expressions of Interest (EOI) to understand the availability, location and readiness of Facilities that may be able to provide System Restart Service across the SWIS.

Previous System Restart Service engagements have indicated that other existing or new Facilities may also be capable of providing System Restart Service, subject to necessary site works, testing and lead times.

AEMO invites Market Participants, or prospective Market Participants, with Facilities capable of providing System Restart Service to make submissions for:

* a Facility with System Restart Service capability to commence from 23 October 2028 (EOI Part 1); and

* a Facility with System Restart Service capability to commence only after October 2030 (EOI Part 2).

AEMO welcomes submissions for either existing or proposed Facilities with different technology configurations to submit an EOI. The EOI will be used by AEMO to determine the requirements of a subsequent tender, such as the location of the service (Sub-Network) and service commencement period.

AEMO will specifically use the information from the EOI to:

* identify a short-list of candidates that are able to meet the System Restart Standard;

* assess the efficacy to provide System Restart Services;

* review and potentially amend the System Restart Standard, including the Electrical Sub-Network boundaries (i.e. this is to determine the location AEMO will be tendering for the System Restart Service); and

* confirm with short-listed candidates any necessary upgrades or capital works to be compliant with the future System Restart Standard and the System Restart Service Specification and identify associated timelines to provide the service.

All submissions:

* must be provided in good faith but are not binding on the respondent; and

* will be treated as confidential information under applicable Electricity System and Market Rules.

Submissions must be provided via VendorPanel in accordance with the EOI Guideline by 5pm AWST on 9 November 2026.

title: Request for Information - Transport Coordination Centre - Technology Capabilities
description:
The Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) invites responses to this Request for Information (RFI) from suppliers of technology products, platforms, data, integration and related services that may support the Transport Coordination Centre (TCC).

The Transport Coordination Centre (TCC) Program is a multi-year TMR transformation initiative to establish a statewide, integrated, multi-modal transport coordination facility and operating model.

TMR will lead the TCC as a multi-modal operations centre that integrates Queensland’s key transport modes, including road, rail, bus, light rail and ferry.

The TCC will oversee real-time network management, optimisation, disruption response, customer communications, demand management, data analysis and performance reporting. Its vision is to enable safer, smoother and more reliable travel for passengers and freight across Queensland through reduced travel times, improved journey reliability, faster incident response, personalised updates, increased freight efficiency and more efficient use of existing transport infrastructure.

The TCC will be established before the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games and will scale to manage Games-time transport demand.

The TCC Program has multiple delivery streams. This RFI is issued by the Technology stream and relates to the operational systems, platforms, data and enabling technology required for the TCC to deliver its services.

description:
Nambucca Valley Council is seeking suitably qualified & experienced tenderers for the Design & Construction of a water main renewal associated with the Little Motleys Bridge Replacement. The Contractor is responsible for the design development and installation of a replacement Trunk Main using HDD techniques as well as inter-connection works at both ends. Integration with the Principals concept design and coordination of Engineering design disciples.

The works included in the Contract comprise the provision of all that is necessary for the complete and proper construction, testing and commissioning of the following, in strict accordance with this Specification, the accompanying Drawings and such other drawings and standards as may be issued from time to time during the progress of the works.

The scope of works includes, but is not limited to the following:

•	Develop concept designs to enable an effective HDD installation beneath Bowra Creek.

•	Supply, construct and commission a water trunk main and all associated connections, valves and fittings.

•	Design and construct interconnections at each end of the main including one isolation valve at each end. Valves to be 450 diameter geared valves with Clockwise Closing convention.

•	Supply, construct and commission of a water trunk main high level scour pit near the eastern connection.

•	Reinstatement of existing surfaces where affected by construction activities.

•	Carry out earthworks as required to provide adequate drainage at each site post construction.

•	Documentation of the works, and

•	All other civil works necessary for satisfactory operation of the water network.

The scope of works is outlined in Attachment 1 Technical Speciation Document

A Geotechnical Assessment would form a component of Contractor Design Development if the contractor chooses to do so.

Geotechnical information (Boreholes 1 & 2) has been captured on the concept plan provided as Attachment 1 and discussed through the commentary in Attachment 3

title: Cairns Marine Precinct - Common User Facility (CMP-CUF) Co-Investment
description:
The Opportunity:

Ports North is pleased to advise that Request for Proposal (RFP) Phase 1 for the Cairns Marine Precinct - Common User Facility (CMP-CUF) Co-Investment Opportunity has now commenced.

Ports North is proposing the development of the Cairns Marine Precinct – Common User Facility, a major maritime infrastructure project, to expand the marine vessel maintenance capability and capacity in Far North Queensland to support the continued growth of the region’s maritime industry. The proposed facility responds to increasing demand for maritime maintenance, repair, and overhaul services as global vessel fleets expand and age, alongside sustained investment in Australia’s maritime defence capability driving long-term sustainment demand.

Ports North has identified a Finance (co-funded), Design, Build, Operate and Maintain (FDBOM) commercial delivery model as the most efficient means of Project delivery to successfully facilitate achievement of the Project Objectives. As the Project will benefit from a significant contribution of funds from the Queensland and Commonwealth Governments, the physical facilities coming into existence as a result of the Project will be a common user facility available for use by the operator and customers including vessel owners and ship maintenance and repair service providers.

Ports North is seeking a private sector proponent to co-fund, develop, operate and maintain the facility under a long-term arrangement on Ports North-owned land at the Port of Cairns.

This RFP follows the successful completion of an Expression of Interest (EOI) process. Participation in the EOI process was not a prerequisite for participation in RFP Phase 1. Ports North welcomes registrations and proposals from organisations that did not participate in the EOI and may be engaging with the opportunity for the first time.

Purpose of this Request for Proposal:

The purpose of this RFP is to elicit proposals from the market that address the Project Objectives and develop the CMP-CUF, including the following:

•	the co-funding of the Project;

•	the design, construction and commissioning of the CMP-CUF; and

•	the operation and maintenance of the CMP-CUF on a common user basis.

How to Participate in RFP Phase 1:

Proposals are being accepted only via the Ansarada CMP-CUF RFP Phase 1 Data Room. Submissions via this Queensland Procurement Solution may not be eligible.

To participate:

- register online via https://www.portsnorth.com.au/ports-north-projects/cairns-marine-precinct

- Shortly after, Ports North will provide access to the Ansarada CMP-CUF RFP Phase 1 Data Room

- Access the RFP documentation within the CMP-CUF RFP Phase 1 Data Room

- Submit your RFP via the CMP-CUF RFP Phase 1 Data Room prior to 1200 AEST on Friday 18 December 2026.

Enquiries regarding the procurement process may be directed to cmpenquiry@portsnorth.com.au.

publicQuestions.question:
Q1: The Project Brief states that Zeal Bridge is to be replaced “like for like”. However, the supplied Level 3 Investigation Report notes that, due to the bridge’s State-level heritage significance, replacement is unlikely to be an available option and recommends conservation, strengthening and renewal of existing elements. Can Council please clarify whether the intended design scope is: (a) complete like-for-like replacement; (b) staged reconstruction retaining significant sandstone/wrought-iron fabric; or (c) rehabilitation/strengthening of the existing structure, with the preferred intervention to be determined through the heritage/options assessment?

Q2: Please confirm Council’s required ultimate functional outcome for Zeal Bridge, including target vehicle/load capacity, whether the existing 15t restriction is to be retained or increased, design speed, required barrier performance level and whether the bridge is to remain single lane. If these matters are to be resolved during the options assessment, please confirm that detailed design will proceed only after Council formally selects the preferred service level.

Q3: For Todds Bridge, can Council please confirm whether there is a preferred side of the existing bridge for the new offline structure and provide any nominated alignment corridor, property/access constraints, land ownership information or minimum separation requirement from the heritage bridge? Alternatively, should the Consultant assess multiple offline alignments and recommend the preferred alignment through the options assessment?

Q4: Will Council provide the editable CAD/design files, digital survey and calculation/model information associated with the previous Todds Bridge replacement design? Please also confirm whether the supplied 2016 geotechnical investigation and previous survey may be relied upon where applicable, subject to the Consultant’s professional review, with only targeted supplementary investigations undertaken for the selected new alignment.

Q5: Please confirm the design criteria to be adopted for each bridge, including design vehicle/loading, design life, design speed, carriageway/lane width, pedestrian provision, barrier performance level, approach-road classification and any Council-specific requirements beyond AS 5100, Austroads and the Infrastructure Design Manual. Council advises that traffic-volume data will be provided at contract award; can indicative traffic data or vehicle composition be made available during the tender period to assist pricing and concept development?

Q6: For Zeal Bridge, is Council expecting intrusive geotechnical investigation and/or exploratory excavation to determine the founding arrangement of the heritage sandstone abutments and central pier as part of the lump-sum scope, or should the need for such intrusive works first be established through the heritage/options assessment and then agreed with Council before proceeding?

Q7: For Todds Bridge, does Council expect the Consultant to allow for a completely new intrusive geotechnical investigation along the new alignment, or should the tender allow for review of the existing 2016 investigation followed by targeted supplementary boreholes/rock coring only where required to support the preferred alignment?

Q8: Please confirm the required utility-location standard for the feature survey. Should the tender include QL-B field locating only, with QL-A potholing/proving limited to identified conflicts, or is Council expecting all potentially affected underground services to be physically proven as part of the base lump sum?

Q9: Please provide any available flood levels, hydraulic models, flood studies, design events and North Central Catchment Management Authority requirements relevant to Forest Creek and the Coliban River. Please confirm that the base scope is limited to NCCMA liaison and assessment using available information, and that any new detailed hydrologic/hydraulic modelling required by NCCMA or Council will be treated as a Council-directed variation in accordance with Section 3.5.

Q10: Please confirm that the base ecological assessment is to comprise the general flora/fauna, native-vegetation and arboricultural assessment described in Section 3.3, and that any targeted or seasonal surveys for threatened species identified as necessary through the initial assessment will be treated as additional services/variation unless specifically listed in Schedule C.

Q11: Does the required ecological scope include preparation and lodgement of statutory vegetation-removal, FFG Act or EPBC Act applications and procurement of biodiversity offsets, or is the Consultant required only to identify the applicable approval pathway, impact/offset requirements and provide a report suitable to support subsequent applications?

Q12: Please confirm that the base lump sum is to include the Phase A desktop cultural heritage assessment only, with the Standard Assessment, Complex Assessment, CHMP and heritage impact/site-inspection items priced separately as Provisional Sum Items and undertaken only following Council’s written direction after the relevant hold point.

Q13: The Project Brief states that RAP participation fees for meetings/fieldwork and the RAP’s CHMP evaluation fee will be paid directly by Council, while other statutory fees are to be paid by the Consultant. Can Council please identify the statutory application/notification fees that are expected to be included within the Consultant’s tendered fee, and confirm that all RAP professional participation and CHMP evaluation charges remain direct Council costs?

Q14: Please confirm whether the lump sum entered in Schedule A is to comprise only the base services, excluding the Schedule C items specifically identified as Provisional Sum Items, or whether Schedule A is intended to include the total of the base services plus all provisional sums. If provisional sums are to be included in the Schedule A figure, please confirm how they will be treated for tender-price/VFM evaluation.

Q15: Schedule C Item 10 for Todds Bridge refers to “Draft detailed design submission and draft cost estimate”, whereas the Project Brief requires a separate technical specification for each bridge. Please confirm that preparation of the draft/final technical specification for Todds Bridge is required and whether it is to be priced under Items 10 and 11 respectively.

Q16: Part Three Section 7 states that the Services and Deliverables are to be provided by 28 June 2027, while Schedule E states that the Contract Works must be fully completed by 31 May 2027. Please confirm the contractual Date for Completion. If 31 May is the technical-design completion milestone, please confirm whether the period to 28 June is intended for administrative, heritage/RAP approval or final close-out activities.

Q17: Can Council confirm the anticipated contract commencement date and whether Council will be available to undertake the specified two-week review of the concept/design report submitted by 5 December 2026, noting that the subsequent draft detailed-design milestone is 15 January 2027? Please advise whether the Christmas/New Year shutdown is to be excluded from Council review periods or whether the published milestone remains unchanged.

Q18: Annexure Part A Item 24 states that the Consultant’s liability is “No Limit”, while the required Professional Indemnity insurance is $5 million. Would Council accept an aggregate liability cap aligned with the required PI insurance limit, or another mutually agreed reasonable monetary cap, subject to customary exclusions for matters such as fraud and wilful misconduct?
publicQuestions.answer:
A1: Design the bridge as is, draft the bridge, and rehabilitation/strengthening of the existing structure, with the preferred intervention to be determined through the heritage/options assessment.

A2: Yes that detailed design will proceed only after Council formally selects the preferred service level.

A3: Consultant assess multiple offline alignments and recommend the preferred alignment through the options assessment.

A4: Council doesn’t have CAD/Design files but PDF versions. The survey is also in pdf format. Consultants will need to survey and design the bridge and provide Council with CAD files and use the existing files as information.

A5: Design according to AS5100, council has no specific requirements. Refer to attached traffic data, but another traffic count will be undertaken shortly.

A6: Yes, you are right should there be a need for such intrusive works first be established through the heritage/options assessment and then agreed with Council before proceeding.

A7: The tender should allow for review of the existing 2016 investigation followed by targeted supplementary boreholes/rock coring only where required to support the preferred alignment.

A8: Council is expecting all potentially affected underground services to be physically proven as part of the base lump sum and should in the plans with actual depths.

A9: There is no modelling, flood studies required for this tender, but consultation with NCCMA is required to obtain the 1% AEP storm event level with freeboard at those locations.

A10: That is correct.

A11: Consultant are required to identify the applicable approval pathway, impact/offset requirements and provide a report suitable to support subsequent applications, however documents must be acceptable to DEECA.

A12: That is correct.

A13: Council will pay for all RAP professional participation and CHMP evaluation charges. There should not be any other statutory application/notification fees.

A14: Yes, provisional sums are to be included in the Schedule A figure, and will be used to evaluate the tender but can’t be expended without prior approval.

A15: Yes that preparation of the draft/final technical specification for Todds Bridge is required and to be priced under Items 10 and 11 respectively.

A16: Yes, 28 June is intended for administrative, heritage/RAP approval or final close-out activities.

A17: The published milestones remain unchanged and the anticipated commencement date is 18 November 2026

A18: Consultants may propose alternatives to the items listed in item 24 of the annexure as a non-conforming tender for consideration. Council may choose to accept or reject any non-conforming tenders.

title: Whitsunday Regional Sports Precinct Stage 1 - Design and Construction
description:
The Whitsunday Regional Council (Principal) is delivering the Whitsunday Regional Sports Precinct (WRSP) to address the increasing demand for high-quality sporting, recreation and community infrastructure across the Whitsunday Region.

The WRSP is one of Council's most significant community infrastructure investments and will provide a contemporary regional sporting destination that supports organised sport, community participation, recreation, health and wellbeing, regional events and long-term population growth. The precinct has been planned to meet current community needs while providing a scalable framework for future expansion through subsequent stages of development.

Stage 1 represents the first phase of the Master Plan and will establish the core sporting facilities, supporting infrastructure and services required to enable the precinct to operate as a high-quality regional sports hub. The completed works are intended to provide durable, functional and maintainable infrastructure that delivers value for money over the life of the asset while supporting a broad range of community users.

This Principal's Project Requirements (PPR) defines the minimum functional, operational, technical and performance requirements for the Project. It establishes the outcomes that the Contractor is required to achieve and forms the basis upon which the Contractor will develop, coordinate, design, construct, commission and hand over the Works.

The Works will be delivered under an AS 4300–1995 Design and Construct Contract, under which the Contractor will assume full responsibility for the detailed design, design coordination, statutory approvals, construction, commissioning, testing and handover of the completed facility, except where expressly stated otherwise in the Contract.

This Project is funded under the Australian Government Growing Regions Program. In accordance with the Project Funding Agreement, the Head Contractor must hold and maintain current accreditation under the Australian Government Work Health and Safety Accreditation Scheme (the Scheme) for the entirety of the Contract.

Tenderers must:

a)	hold current accreditation under the Australian Government Work Health and Safety Accreditation Scheme at the Tender Closing Time;

b)	provide evidence of current accreditation with their Tender submission;

c)	maintain accreditation for the duration of the Contract, including any extensions of time or defects liability period where accreditation is required to remain in force; and

d)	immediately notify the Principal of any actual or proposed suspension, lapse, cancellation or variation to their accreditation status.

A non-mandatory Tender Site Briefing will be held on Tuesday, 6 October 2026, 1.30 pm (AEST). The location of the meeting will commence at Proserpine Administration Building, 83-85 Main Street, Proserpine Qld 4800 and will progress to the Site Visit at Shute Harbour Road and Brandy Creek Road. Access to the Site is adjacent to the bus stop pair refer to the Conditions of Tender clause 7 for a map for parking at the Site.

N.B. PPE is a requirement to attend this site, at a minimum Hi-Vis long-sleeved shirt, full length pants, steel cap boots and eye protection, it is also recommended to wear sun protection.

Please confirm your attendance at this meeting via contracts@whitsundayrc.qld.gov.au no later than midday, Thursday, 1 October 2026.

All communications must go through the VendorPanel communications forum.

title: Aquatic Wheelchair Replacement
description:
Council seeks the supply and delivery of replacement of 2 x aquatic wheelchairs for use across aquatic and leisure facilities. The replacement equipment must provide safe, reliable and accessible pool entry and exit for patrons with limited mobility, while being suitable for use in wet, chlorinated environments.

Minimum Requirements

The supplied aquatic wheelchair must:

•	Be specifically designed for pool / hydrotherapy and wet-area environments.

•	Be constructed from corrosion-resistant and rustproof materials suitable for continuous exposure to water and outdoor conditions.

•	Be lightweight, durable and easy to manoeuvre for both users and carers.

•	Include solid, puncture-proof tyres and hand-operated brakes on both rear wheels.

•	Provide a comfortable and safe seating arrangement suitable for aquatic facility patrons.

•	Be capable of being fully immersed in water, via a lifting frame

•	Be compatible with the existing Pelican Pool/Spa Hoist system currently in use at Council’s Hydrotherapy Centre.

•	Allow safe transfer of patrons into and out of pools when used in conjunction with the hoist system, including a restraint/seat belt

•	Have a safe working load of 200kgs

•	Comply with relevant Australian safety and accessibility standards.

Preferred Solution

The preferred replacement is the Platypus Pool and Wet Area Wheelchair manufactured by Para Mobility, or an equivalent approved alternative that meets all functional and compatibility requirements.

Deliverables

The successful supplier shall provide:

•	Supply and delivery of the aquatic wheelchair(s). Address: 4 Creek Road St Marys NSW 2760.

•	Manufacturer specifications and warranty information.

•	Operating and maintenance instructions.

•	Confirmation of compatibility with the existing Pelican Pool/Spa Hoist system.

Evaluation Criteria

Submissions will be assessed on:

•	Compliance with the minimum requirements.

•	Compatibility with existing infrastructure and equipment.

•	Product durability and suitability for aquatic environments.

•	Warranty, support and availability of replacement parts.

•	Overall value for money.

publicQuestions.question:
Morning Michael,

Thank you for providing the EOI documentation, we're very interested in assisting council deliver their Western Sydney Infrastructure Grants Program projects throughout 2027 and 2028. We have a few initial questions, please see below:

- Does council have any information on the type of projects that make up the portfolio (are they road projects, water network, water treatment, other facilities projects etc)?

- Does council require only civil based resources, or do they require a mix of disciplines (mechanical, electrical, control systems, structures etc) to service the projects?

- Linked to our question above, and referring to Schedule 1 of the returnable schedules, if multi discipline expertise is required, does council welcome different rates for individuals from differing discipline backgrounds?

- In delivering the project management services, does council have an expectation for personnel to be physically in council's offices, or are remote based personnel welcomed? (Noting superintendent engagements would need to be site based).

We look forward to receiving your response.
publicQuestions.answer:
Council’s Major Projects webpage includes information on all the current large scale projects that we are delivering. In general this Panel will support civil projects – pathways and town centre upgrades. Other types of projects may be added over the life of the panel, however BMCC does not have water and sewer responsibilities.

At the moment we require civil based project management services, we have no projects at this time that would require mechanical, electrical, control systems etc.

Yes, council welcomes different rates from individuals with different backgrounds or different levels of experience.

Council is not requiring consultants work from our offices, though we may require on site attendance at workshops on occasion. This will be outlined in the individual works packages to be released to the panel so that it can be costed if required. Engagements as the Superintendents Representative will require attendance on site.

publicQuestions.question:

publicQuestions.question:

publicQuestions.question:

title: Expression of Interest - Southern Water Treatment Plant Project
description:
Toowoomba Regional Council (Council) is one of Queensland’s largest regional Councils, serving approximately 184,000 people across a geographical area of 12,973 square kilometres. Located in South East Queensland, approximately 125 kilometres west of Brisbane, the Region encompasses the city of Toowoomba, the regional centres of Oakey, Pittsworth, Millmerran, Highfields, Crows Nest, Clifton, Greenmount and Yarraman, and numerous smaller townships.

Council is responsible for delivering and maintaining essential community infrastructure and services, including water, wastewater, waste, drainage, roads, bridges, footpaths, utilities and recreational facilities. Through its Water and Waste Services Group, Council manages the Region’s water treatment, storage and distribution assets, including the existing Mount Kynoch Water Treatment Plant (WTP).

Water security is fundamental to supporting the continued growth and prosperity of the Toowoomba Region. The construction of the Queensland Government’s Toowoomba

to Warwick Pipeline (T2WP) has created an opportunity for the Toowoomba region to benefit in exchange for the use of Council’s raw water infrastructure. Studies on the impact of the T2WP have identified an opportunity to construct a new Southern Water Treatment Plant (SWTP), now an initiative within the Toowoomba Regional Council Water Vision 2021–2071.

It involves a new plant of at least 25 ML/d capacity that will provide a reliable water source for the region to ensure long-term water security and support regional growth. The

new SWTP will facilitate population growth in the southern and western regions of Toowoomba by providing a new water source and alleviating the demands currently placed

on the Mt Kynoch WTP. Raw water for the new WTP is proposed to be taken from an offtake from the T2WP. Additional distribution assets to service the new WTP

include a 15 ML reservoir in the Mt Peel Bushland Reserve, a pump station, 15 km of trunk and distribution pipelines and other pipeline structures.

The Project will enhance the Region’s long-term water security, improve network capacity and resilience, and provide reliable water services to support existing communities and future population growth, particularly across the southern and western areas of Toowoomba.

Council seeks EOI Responses from suitably qualified and experienced Contractors with capability and capacity to deliver the scope of works detailed within this document.

The purpose of this Request for EOI is to:

- advise the market of the project and provide an overview of the likely scope of works

- describe the procurement process including indicative timeline for delivery of the Project

- provide an overview of the proposed commercial and legal framework

- enable Council to shortlist down to potentially two (2) suitably qualified Proponents to proceed to the Early Contractor Involvement (ECI) Phase of the evaluation process.

title: ITT265 - IT Service Management
description:
Sunshine Coast Council is seeking to implement a modern, integrated ITSM platform to replace the current service management environment and provide a scalable foundation for improved technology service delivery. The project will initially focus on delivering a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) for core ITSM capabilities, including incident, request, change, problem, knowledge, service catalogue, service level management and reporting. The solution must also provide a clear pathway to expand into Enterprise Service Management (ESM), Software Asset Management (SAM), Configuration Management Database (CMDB) capability and controlled IT documentation management. The project is intended to improve service visibility, process consistency, user experience, operational reporting, asset and configuration intelligence, and Council’s ability to manage technology services in a controlled, sustainable and continuously improving manner.

The objectives of this procurement are to:

• Replace Council’s incumbent ITSM platform approaching end-of-life.

• Deliver core ITSM functionality rapidly via MVP.

• Provide a scalable platform for enterprise-wide service management.

• Establish a reliable SAM capability to improve licence compliance, software cost visibility and renewal planning.

• Establish a governed CMDB capability to improve change impact assessment, incident resolution and service dependency visibility.

• Provide a controlled IT documentation repository for systems, applications, vendors, credentials references, runbooks, SOPs and support procedures.

• Enable internal capability uplift for ongoing configuration, administration and continuous improvement.

The initial Term of this Contract will be for a period of 5 years, with 3 x 12 month extension options.

Funding has been approved under the DRFA program to restore eligible public assets that were directly damaged by the disaster events. RFI01 - EOT Request

Hi Julianne,

We respectfully request an Extension of Time (EOT) for the submission of our tender for the Sludge Dewatering Upgrade Project, extending the current submission deadline of 5 November 2026 to 20 November 2026.

This extension is requested to allow sufficient time to obtain and assess vendor package pricing, receive outstanding subcontractor quotations, and develop a complete and accurate tender submission that adequately addresses the complexities and various elements of the project.

The current tender timeframe has presented several challenges, including:

•	Vendor package pricing and lead times: The specialised nature of the sludge dewatering equipment requires engagement with multiple vendors to obtain compliant technical and commercial offers. Allowing sufficient time for vendors to review the project requirements and develop their submissions is essential.

•	Subcontractor responses: A number of subcontractor quotations remain outstanding, with additional time required to obtain, review and clarify pricing to ensure all relevant scope elements are adequately covered.

•	Limited supplier participation: Several suppliers have declined to provide pricing due to the short turnaround time available. This has restricted the number of competitive quotations received and increased the time required to identify and engage alternative suppliers.

•	Project complexity and scope coordination: The project involves multiple interfacing elements, vendor packages and subcontracted works that require careful coordination to ensure the proposed solution is technically compliant and commercially complete.

•	Tender accuracy and completeness: Additional time is required to review vendor and subcontractor submissions, reconcile scope gaps and exclusions, confirm pricing assumptions, and undertake a detailed internal review of the estimate and overall tender submission.

The requested extension will provide the necessary opportunity to obtain more complete and reliable pricing, properly assess the associated risks and exclusions, and ensure our final submission represents an accurate and considered offer that meets the project requirements.

title: Tender for land within the Lansdown Eco-Industrial Precinct
description:
The Lansdown Eco-Industrial Precinct (LEIP or Precinct) is positioned as a major industrial precinct for environmentally responsible advanced manufacturing, technology and processing activities. The Precinct is located approximately 40 kilometres south of the Townsville central business district in the suburb of Calcium and comprises approximately 2,200 hectares extending east from the Mingela State Forest and Lansdown Creek towards the Flinders Highway. Townsville City Council (Council) acquired the land in 2001 after its previous use by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation as a pasture research site.

LEIP is supported by strategic access to the Port of Townsville, major road and rail corridors, the North Queensland Gas Pipeline, the Woodstock Ergon Substation and planned industrial water infrastructure. Since 2019, Council has undertaken several open market processes for land within the Precinct. Those processes resulted in conditional land allocations across advanced manufacturing, energy, critical minerals, storage, chemical processing and related projects. This refreshed market land tender considers remaining available land with the LEIP.

title: RFT(EXC00136) Flood and River Level Monitoring Services for Townsville City Council
description:
Townsville City Council requires a vendor led solution under Stream B of the Enviromon Replacement project. The solution must replace the operational capability currently provided by Enviromon and TARDIS for the receipt, processing, storage, visualisation, alerting, reporting and onward distribution of flood warning observation data.

Council currently relies on ALERT rainfall and water level gauge data to support disaster management, flood modelling, situational awareness and operational decision making across the Townsville Local Government Area. The Bureau of Meteorology has advised that support for Enviromon will cease in October 2026, and TARDIS is expected to reach end of support in 2027. The replacement solution must therefore provide a sustainable, secure and future ready capability that supports continuity of Council’s flood warning data operations before legacy support risks become unacceptable.

The Supplier must provide a commercially available, configurable cloud SaaS solution and associated implementation services. The Supplier must not propose a tactical in house build as the primary solution. The intent of this Scope is to obtain a mature, supportable and secure platform that can be implemented, tested, transitioned into operation and supported under agreed service levels.

publicQuestions.question: Subcontractors: Council's ITT 2.17 requires its approval of subcontractors. Can Council confirm it will accept a principal contractor that uses approved Victorian civil, asphalt and traffic management subcontractors for the works, with each one submitted for approval before engagement?
publicQuestions.answer:
Yes. Council will accept a principal contractor that engages suitably qualified subcontractors for civil, asphalt and traffic management works, provided that each proposed subcontractor is submitted to Council for review and approval prior to engagement. Approval of the principal contractor does not constitute approval of its subcontractors, and no subcontractor may be engaged until Council's approval has been obtained in accordance with Clause 2.17 of the ITT.

The principal contractor remains responsible for the performance and compliance of all approved subcontractors.
