publicQuestions.question:
Hi Marcio,

I’m Kieran Shirey, founder of LOGiT Australia, an Aboriginal-owned business developing Kin-Neon (kinneon.au), a housing production approach intended to build local manufacturing, assembly and maintenance capability.

Our development work includes mobile production of interlocking stabilised earth blocks, with any use of local materials subject to suitability testing, engineering and the required approvals. We are investigating ways to reduce transport, labour and external contractor dependency while building lasting community capability.

Having reviewed the tender’s provisions for alternative materials and construction systems, we would appreciate clarification on a potential specialist role alongside an appropriately qualified D&C contractor:

1. What technical evidence and approvals must be available at tender submission for an alternative wall or material system, and what may be completed during the subsequent design and approval stages?

2. Would Council and DHPW consider a limited, engineer-reviewed component within a conforming delivery proposal, supported by a fully compliant fallback so that housing delivery does not depend on unresolved R&D? We understand that a non-conforming alternative must accompany a conforming tender.

3. For a specialist participating through a lead D&C contractor, must the specialist also attend the mandatory site visit, or can the lead contractor’s attendance satisfy that requirement?

4. If the development stage makes participation in this tender premature, is there an appropriate separate pathway for discussing a future demonstration or training project? We would follow Council’s nominated process for any such discussion.

5. Please confirm the supplier-question deadline. The Request Summary states 6 November 2026 at 2 pm AEST, while Part A clause 5.10(c) contains different wording and a reference to 6 October.

We are seeking clarification of the appropriate participation and evidence requirements at this stage. We are not representing Kin-Neon as a certified system or offering to undertake the turnkey D&C scope independently.
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Technical evidence and approvals

At tender submission, proponents should provide sufficient technical information to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed system and its ability to meet the Principal's Requirements, including structural performance, cyclone resistance, durability, thermal performance, maintainability and applicable DHPW standards.

Detailed engineering, testing and statutory certification may be completed during the subsequent design development and approval stages, where appropriate. However, any proposed system must have a credible pathway to compliance, and the successful D&C contractor remains responsible for obtaining all necessary approvals and certifications before construction.

2. Limited application and compliant fallback

Council is open to considering innovative materials or construction systems as part of a conforming D&C proposal, including their limited application to suitable building components.

A fully compliant fallback solution may assist in managing delivery risk. However, any proposed alternative must be clearly identified and supported by sufficient technical evidence to enable its assessment. Council cannot provide advance acceptance of an untested or uncertified system, and any proposed solution would remain subject to the applicable design review, engineering and statutory approval requirements.

3. Mandatory site visit

The mandatory site visit requirement applies to the Tenderer submitting the D&C proposal. Where a specialist participates as a subcontractor or consultant to a Principal Contractor, the Principal Contractor's attendance will satisfy this requirement. Specialist participation in the site visit is encouraged where it would assist with understanding site conditions and delivery requirements.

4. Future demonstration or training opportunities

Council recognises the potential value of initiatives that develop local manufacturing, construction and maintenance capabilities.

Should participation in the current procurement be premature, you are welcome to submit a separate proposal for Council's consideration outside the current tender process. Any future demonstration or training initiative would be subject to Council's priorities, available funding, applicable approvals and procurement requirements.

5. Clarification deadline

I confirm that the deadline for tender enquiries is 2:00 pm (AEST) on 6 November 2026, as stated in the VendorPanel Request Summary. The reference to 6 October in Part A is an administrative error, which Council will clarify through VendorPanel.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi Marcio,

Thank you for suggesting I introduce my proposal to the D&C contractors tendering for Palm Island via Vendor Panel. I am an Australian architect with work spanning tropical Queensland to the Tasmanian highlands, and a particular interest in creating pragmatic, economical yet traditionally beautiful buildings and places. As an example, my open-source Tasmanian House model shows how distinctive, characterful homes can be delivered at exceptionally low cost, as documented by ABC News and other publications. During my postgraduate studies I also worked in the Aboriginal town camps of Alice Springs, gaining firsthand experience of the challenges of remote-community housing. Further examples of my work, including alternative masterplans advocating locally characteristic, picturesque and human-scaled settlements, can be found at www.lev.au and www.jirilev.au.

I believe Palm Island presents a wonderful opportunity to establish a new model for social housing, demonstrating that homes can satisfy every technical requirement, including Gold Level accessibility, durability, climatic comfort and affordability, while also contributing to beautiful streetscapes and a genuinely loved township. Some of the island's older high-set houses, generous verandahs and lattice screens already offer lovely precedents.

I would be interested in working with a Principal Contractor to study and evolve this local architectural tradition, creating varied but harmonious houses, gardens and public spaces that contribute to residents' happiness, satisfaction and pride in their community. I believe much could be achieved through thoughtful design without necessarily increasing construction costs. Palm Island could become a nationally significant example of social housing that people are proud to call home and that visitors find attractive and memorable.

Could Council please confirm:

1. May Principal Contractors engage an independent architect to further develop and improve the architectural character, appearance, site layouts and streetscapes of the reference designs, provided all budgetary, functional, accessibility and technical requirements are maintained?

2. May these architectural improvements be included in a contractor's tender proposal and developed further in consultation with Council and the community following appointment?

I would welcome enquiries from interested contractors, whether for an individual package or the wider programme. My involvement could be tailored to their existing teams, programmes and budgets.

Kind regards,

Jiri Lev, architect - jiri@lev.au
publicQuestions.answer:
Council welcomes design enhancements proposed by tenderers, including through the engagement of independent architects, provided all functional, technical, accessibility, budgetary and other tender requirements are met.

Proposed enhancements may be included in tender submissions and will be considered as part of the evaluation process. Any further design development following contract award will be subject to Council approval and the contract requirements.

publicQuestions.question:
Good afternoon,

Regarding Lots 60A, 60B, 60C and 60D, Thiday Road, Butler Bay, we note that the sites have significant tree coverage.

publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

1. Responsibility for vegetation clearing

Vegetation clearing required to undertake the proposed development is to be included within the Principal Contractor's Design and Construct (D&C) scope. Council does not intend to undertake vegetation clearing prior to construction.

2. Vegetation clearing approvals

Council is responsible for obtaining the applicable development and planning approvals. The Principal Contractor will be responsible for identifying vegetation clearing requirements, undertaking the necessary investigations and securing any additional permits or approvals associated with its construction methodology, where required.

Tenderers should allow for the necessary vegetation clearing works and associated costs within their submissions.

publicQuestions.question:
Good morning Council,

Following on from the teams meeting, I have a couple questions.

Q1. As mentioned in the meeting, you would look at multiple contracts for this project, would you accept delivery to the port only?

Q1. If yes to Q1, would a site inspection be mandatory?

Thank you.
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your questions.

Q1. Would Council accept delivery to the port only?

No. While Council may award separate contracts for individual housing packages, each contract must cover the full Design and Construct (D&C) scope, including transportation to Palm Island, on-site construction, commissioning, certification and handover.

Proposals limited to supply and delivery to the port will not be accepted as conforming tenders.

Q2. Would a site inspection be mandatory if only delivering to the port?

As supply-and-delivery-only proposals are not accepted, this question is not applicable. The mandatory site inspection requirement remains applicable to all D&C tenderers.

publicQuestions.question:
Regarding vegetation clearing for Package 5, Lots 60A–60D, please provide any available clearing and tree-retention plans, vegetation assessments and applicable approval conditions.

Please also confirm:

- The required clearing extent, including building footprints, access, services and construction working areas.

- Requirements for stump removal, grubbing, backfilling and retained-tree protection.

- Whether on-site chipping or retention of mulch is permitted, and the approved disposal options for vegetation and stumps.

- Whether a separately identified provisional sum for clearing would be accepted where the extent or approval requirements remain unresolved at tender close. If not, please nominate the pricing basis tenderers should adopt.
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

1. Vegetation clearing plans and assessments

Council has not provided a separate vegetation clearing or tree-retention plan for Package 5. Tenderers are required to assess existing site conditions during the mandatory site inspection and make appropriate allowances in their submissions.

2. Extent of clearing

The Principal Contractor is responsible for determining the vegetation clearing required to deliver the proposed dwellings, including building footprints, access, services and construction working areas. Clearing should be limited to what is reasonably necessary for the development, subject to applicable approvals and environmental requirements.

3. Stump removal and tree protection

The D&C scope includes all necessary stump removal, grubbing, backfilling, ground preparation and protection of retained vegetation. These works must be undertaken in accordance with applicable standards and approval conditions.

4. Vegetation disposal

On-site chipping and reuse of mulch may be proposed, subject to Council acceptance and applicable environmental requirements. Tenderers are responsible for identifying suitable and lawful disposal arrangements for vegetation and stumps and including the associated costs in their submissions.

5. Pricing basis

Tenderers are required to include vegetation clearing and associated site preparation costs within their lump-sum tender price. A separately identified provisional sum is not proposed for these works.

Tenderers should base their pricing on the reference designs, available site information and their own site investigations, clearly identifying any assumptions made.

description:
As the Managing Contractor for Integrated Land Target System (ILTS) Program, ATS will be responsible for the procurement, delivery into service, inventory management, replenishment and sustainment (where applicable) of live-fire target Consumable Aluminium Target products for the Department of Defence (Defence).

The Integrated Land Target System (ILTS) Program defines a means by which Defence can improve, modernise and enhance land combatant training outcomes through contemporary and fit for purpose target systems and Consumables, managed and sustained under the Program.

This Statement of Requirement (SOR) defines the requirement for the establishment of a Standing Offer for the supply of Consumable Aluminium Target products in support of Army training activities. The products to be supplied are used on Defence training ranges to enable the safe, realistic and effective conduct of live-fire weapons training. The products will be engaged with live ammunition and are expected to be replaced as a result of ballistic damage, weathering and normal range wear.

The Consumable Aluminium Target products must provide clear visual definition and consistent engagement characteristics, and must be suitable for use with the weapon systems and ammunition types where specified in this tender. As Consumables, they are required to be cost-effective, available in relevant volumes and supplied to support sustained and surge training demand.

Further information is contained in the tender documentation.

Located in the heart of Western Sydney and in one of the fastest growing areas of New South Wales, the Diocese of Parramatta comprises 80 vibrant and dynamic school communities that stretch from Dundas Valley, north to Richmond, west to Katoomba and south to Luddenham.

There are 58 primary schools and 24 secondary schools and two trade pathway campuses supporting approximately 46,000 students and almost 5,000 staff.

Parish priests, principals and school communities work together to provide faith-filled, radically inclusive and caring environments that allow young people to grow in their faith and better understand the mission of the Church. This is achieved through religious education, faith formation, liturgical celebrations, sacramental programs, pastoral care and support.

Mossman transition plan: The RFQ notes the closure of the Mossman Mill and the need to support workforce transition, economic diversification and regional resilience. Could Council please confirm whether the proposed Marine Industry Precinct is intended to align with, support or implement any recommendations from the Mossman Transition Plan/Study or related economic transition initiatives? Design requirements: The deliverables outlined in the scope, including the requirement to develop three concept plans and a preferred master plan, appear to be consistent with a scoping-level study rather than detailed design. publicQuestions.answer:
QUESTION:

Mossman transition plan: The RFQ notes the closure of the Mossman Mill and the need to support workforce transition, economic diversification and regional resilience. Could Council please confirm whether the proposed Marine Industry Precinct is intended to align with, support or implement any recommendations from the Mossman Transition Plan/Study or related economic transition initiatives? If so, could Council please provide any relevant reports, studies, strategic plans or outputs that respondents should consider in preparing their submissions?

ANSWER:

Council does not currently have a finalised Mossman Transition Plan or equivalent strategy available for respondents to reference. The Marine Industry Precinct study is intended to investigate opportunities for economic diversification and regional resilience, including the potential role of the marine industry in further supporting the local economy.

QUESTION:

Marine industry precinct vessels: Could Council please clarify the intended operational use case for the proposed Marine Industry Precinct? In particular, what vessel types and approximate vessel sizes (length, beam and draft) are anticipated to access and utilise the precinct, including any assumptions regarding commercial, tourism, recreational or superyacht vessels? This information will help inform our assessment of infrastructure requirements, marine engineering considerations and precinct layout.

ANSWER:

The precinct is intended to provide a core facility servicing maritime tourism operators, the commercial fishing fleet and recreational boat owners. The study is intended to investigate the feasibility and potential configuration of the facility, including identifying the maximum vessel sizes that could be accommodated and operate effectively within the area. Respondents should consider the range of potential vessel types and associated infrastructure requirements as part of their assessment.

QUESTION:

Design requirements: The deliverables outlined in the scope, including the requirement to develop three concept plans and a preferred master plan, appear to be consistent with a scoping-level study rather than detailed design. Could Council please confirm whether respondents are expected to undertake Design Work and prepare Design Documents as defined in Section 2 (Design Services), or whether the intended deliverables are limited to concept-level plans and supporting documentation suitable for strategic planning, stakeholder engagement and future funding applications?

ANSWER:

The project is a planning study only, and detailed design is not required. The three concept plans are expected to be developed to a sufficient level of detail to enable Council to assess the options and select a preferred concept. The preferred concept is then to be further refined and incorporated into the final reports to support future planning, stakeholder engagement, and potential funding applications.

Following attendance at todays site tender meeting, can you please provide a response to the following questions/queries:

1. Amenities building (SP2): The spec needs a building built to architectural drawings that aren't in the pack. Will they be issued? Who designs it, and what size and fit-out?

2. Blank-quantity BoQ rows: SP1 rows 164, 195 and 198, and SP2 rows 100, 175, 212, 222, 258, 265 and 270 have no quantity. Are these intended to be priced, and at what quantity? SP1 rows 59–61 and 75 are also "as required".

3. Cell 2.4 to 3.1 interface: Part D says "connection and make good to existing leachate system" and drawings 040, 041, 060 and 061 show an interface, bund and tie-in. There is no BoQ row, so what is the extent of the work and where do we price it?

4. Liner design basis: The EIS describes a double composite liner but the IFC spec and BoQ show a single GCL plus HDPE. Confirm the IFC governs.

5. Cushion geotextile: Table 8.1 (550 g/m²) is "for tendering only". What do we price? If the ASTM D5514 test requires a heavier product, is that a variation?

6.Laps and wastage: The BoQ says "no allowance for overlaps or wastage". Confirm quantities are net and that laps (GCL 300/500 mm, HDPE 100 mm) and roll waste sit within our rates.

7. Stockpile capacity (Attachment K):

a. The concept capacity is about 676,000 m³ but total excavation is about 651,000 bank m³, which swells/bulks.

b. Where does the spoil surplus go?

c. Is any off-site disposal required?

d. Who owns the excavated material, and can it be used as engineered fill?

8. Excavation quantities and geotech:

a. The SP2 BoQ says 190,900 m³ but the EIS says 206,100 m³. Does the BoQ govern?

b. Please issue the geotechnical report, groundwater levels, and expected rock.

c. How are the 9–12 m deep perimeter trenches and dewatering to be managed?

9. Site access and traffic: Is a second track-out control or wheel wash expected? Part D mentions wheel wash, rumble bars or confined access.

10. Contract and programme:

a. A $7.4M development application was reported as lodged on 28 September. Are conditions of consent to be priced in?

b. Attachment J (CAD files) wasn't in our pack, and Part C (base AS4000-2025 conditions) isn't in the tender documents. Please supply both, or confirm AS4000-2025 applies unamended apart from the Annexure.

c. Part A 5.11 says bank guarantees are lodged before commencement, but the Annexure says within 14 days of Date of Contract. Which governs?

d. Can LDs be capped, or limited to Contractor-caused delay?

e. Part B2 has formula errors (SP1 F42, F45, F52; SP2 F31, F62, F73, F178). Will Council issue a corrected workbook, or can we lodge with repairs marked?

a. The spec says the CQA Engineer, GTA, GITA and GMTA are engaged by the Principal, but also says NATA labs do "all" testing "as required under the Contract". Who pays for which tests?

b. Who pays for re-tests and standby when a hold point isn't released? Spec 1.7 says Council isn't liable for standby, so what are the release times?

c. What does Council want in the integrity survey support (isolation, electrodes, water truck, repairs)?

12. Site, services and environment:

a. Water and power:

- Part D says water by cart, but the spec refers to an "extension of the existing on-site reticulation" for the safety shower.

- Where is the connection point and its capacity?

- Part 15 lists power from the existing main switchboard and the leachate pond pump shed. Where are these, and how long are the routes? Drawing 405 shows them.

c. Access road changes: Spec 1.10 says the access road may move at no extra cost and we maintain it. When is it provided, in what condition, and how much notice do we get of changes?

d. Existing assets: Where are the existing leachate pipework, monitoring wells and services? Are potholing and relocations covered, or are we liable for make good under 1.11 and 1.12?

f. Hours: Are Saturday or extended hours possible? What are the EPA licence limits on noise and dust?

a. Spec 14.10 lets us use the Lorentz Pump Scanner controller or a PLC with HMI. Is Lorentz acceptable, and is SCADA integration required? Spec 14.11 only asks for space and inputs in the panels.

b. Who carries the hazardous-area assessment under AS 60079?

c. The spec requires three 50 kL groundwater tanks in SP2 and the BoQ has two. Which governs?

title: Tender 10-27 Design and Construct Boardwalk Jeffery Court, Agnes Water
description:
Gladstone Regional Council (GRC) requires a suitably qualified Contractor to undertake the Design and Construct of an Australian-manufactured fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) Boardwalk located along Jeffery Court, Agnes Water. The boardwalk is to be approximately 90m in length with a width varying between 2.8 - 3.2m, including handrail sections (as required) as detailed in this scope of work. The design shall insure that static electricity buildup across the boardwalk and load bearing members and foundation is adequately addressed. The contractor is responsible for the full design, RPEQ engineering certification, construction, site supervision and provision of as constructed drawings upon completion. '

The boardwalk must be designed and built to retain the existing trees, including avoiding damage to the trunks, roots and critical root zones as defined throughout this document. The project also includes the design and installation of xeric (low-water, drought tolerant) coastal landscaping to enhance amenity and provide a low maintenance interface around the boardwalk. The landscaping must be designed to thrive without irrigation.

As an alternative offer, the Contractor may provide a price for the Design and Construct of the new boardwalk utilising alternative composite materials (such as APR). Where such an alternative offer is presented, the contractor shall ensure that static electricity buildup across the boardwalk surface and load bearing members and foundation is adequately addressed.

publicQuestions.question: Tender 10-27 — Tenderer questions relating to construction program has been raised with Council responses as seen in below response
publicQuestions.answer:
Question 1. Please clarify the exact school-holiday shutdown dates applicable to this contract, including whether both Queensland and NSW holiday periods apply throughout construction or only when determining site possession.

Answer 1: School Holidays applicable:

Qld: 26/03/20027 – 11/04/2027 and 26/06/2027 – 11/07/2027

NSW: 12/04/20027 – 23/04/2027 and 05/07/2027 – 16/07/2027

For clarity, site work can commence 27/04/2027 (Monday 26/04/2027 is observed ANZAC day) and must be complete by 25/06/2027.

Question 2. That the construction period is measured in permitted site working days, excluding weekends unless expressly approved, applicable public/local show holidays, and Council-required school-holiday shutdowns.

Answer 2: Yes.

Question 3. If the programme crosses a prohibited holiday period, the working-day count pauses and resumes on the next permitted working day, with the contractual completion date adjusted accordingly.

Answer 3: Work will not commence on site if the planned duration of the work exceeds the number of working days (plus contingency float) remaining before the next school holiday. The work must be completed in one term, and work shall not be left unfinished over the school holiday (subject to Extension of Time events). The April 2027 site possession date is an estimate of how long it will take to complete site investigation, detail design and procurement of materials prior to the contractor being ready to construct. Construction shall then take place in term time as noted above and completed before the next school holiday. There are 9 working weeks (43 days) available to complete the work.

Question 4. How the stated early-July 2027 completion requirement is intended to operate given that Queensland school holidays commence on 26 June 2027. Please confirm whether construction must finish before that shutdown or may resume afterwards.

Answer 4: As noted above, construction must be complete before the 26 June 2027 School holiday (for clarity, last permitted day of work will be 25/06/2027). Contractor will then have a week to finalise and submit the MDR and as-built documentation.

Question 5. Whether landscape watering, establishment/monitoring visits, safety inspections and emergency protective work are permitted during shutdowns, and what site clearance, security and remobilisation arrangements Council requires.

Answer 5: Watering and establishment visits, along with safety inspections will be permitted during the school holiday period if disruption to the public is kept to a minimum. Emergency works will be permitted as required.

description:
Mount Alexander Shire Council ('Council') are seeking to engage a suitably qualified consultant to deliver and undertake a comprehensive flood study and develop conceptual design/s for flood mitigation solutions along Main Road (and adjacent tributaries) in Campbells Creek township.

The successful consultant will provide specialist expertise in flood modelling, hydraulic and hydrologic assessment, climate change adaptation, planning and conceptual engineering design to improve understanding of flood behaviour within the Campbells Creek catchment, including the interaction between riverine flooding, stormwater runoff and tributary flows.

The consultant will define the existing flood behaviour in the study area and the identification and evaluation of measures to mitigate and manage flood risk in the study area – including, but not limited to, recommendations for flood planning overlays, reviewing the performance of existing drainage, investigating potential mitigation works and updating emergency management plans.

title: Wildlife Detection Technology
description:
Request for Information (RFI) – TMRICTRFI26178 Wildlife Detection Technology.

TMR is seeking information on available and emerging solutions that support a range of capabilities associated with wildlife management in road environments. The capabilities are divided into four core pillars: Detection, Identification, Monitoring and Alerting. At a high level, TMR is interested in identifying technologies that can fully or partially support the four pillars:

1. the automated detection of wildlife near the State Road Network.

2. automated wildlife classification and identification. (accurate identification of wildlife species)

3. automated monitoring of wildlife road-crossing activity and/or in proximity to road infrastructure.

4. the automated generation of real-time alerts/notifications/warnings when wildlife is detected on or near road environments/corridors, together with reporting and analytics to support driver awareness.

vendorPanelDetails.background:
Wildlife–vehicle collisions are an ongoing challenge across road networks and can present safety risks to road users, contribute to wildlife injury and mortality, and create operational, maintenance and environmental management impacts.

While static wildlife warning signs are deployed across parts of the State Road Network to warn drivers to the potential presence of wildlife, their effectiveness in influencing driver behaviour or reducing collision incidents may be limited.

As part of its ongoing commitment to improving road safety outcomes and exploring innovative approaches to network management, TMR is investigating the current state of wildlife detection and driver warning technologies. Advances in sensing, monitoring, communications and artificial intelligence technologies may provide opportunities to improve the real-time detection of wildlife on or near roads and support more targeted warnings to drivers.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes: Through this market engagement, TMR aims to better understand the range of technologies currently available, emerging industry capabilities, and potential future applications that may assist in addressing wildlife-vehicle collision risks across the transport network.

The lighting for Jubilee stadium states 1800 lux average suitable for NRL and AFC UHD Broadcast but no specification provided

would it be right to assume AFC Lighting lighting category 3 standard is to be followed for our design?
publicQuestions.answer:
Dear Supplier,

The design shall achieve a minimum maintained average horizontal illuminance of 1,800 lux across the playing field. For the AFC component, the Category B lighting criteria in the AFC Stadium Regulations, Edition 2026, shall form the minimum benchmark.

The design must also satisfy applicable NRL and UHD broadcast requirements, including camera illuminance, uniformity, glare, colour rendering and flicker performance. AFC Lighting Category 3 shall not be assumed to satisfy all these requirements.

Tenderers shall identify their proposed design criteria and provide lighting calculations demonstrating compliance.

Council

The replacement screen shall provide a native display resolution of at least 3,840 × 2,160 pixels. Supporting a UHD input signal through the processor alone does not satisfy this requirement.

Changes to the active display area or aspect ratio may be proposed for Council’s assessment, provided the tender’s performance requirements are met and compatibility with the existing support structure is demonstrated.

Tenderers shall specify the proposed active display dimensions, native resolution, pixel pitch, aspect ratio and arrangements for displaying 16:9 content without distortion.

Structural assessment and certification shall address the proposed screen, connections and associated loads.

Council

description:
As the Managing Contractor for Integrated Land Target System (ILTS) Program, ATS will be responsible for the procurement, delivery into service, inventory management, replenishment and sustainment (where applicable) Corrugated Target System Consumable products for the Department of Defence (Defence).

The Integrated Land Target System (ILTS) Program defines a means by which Defence can improve, modernise and enhance land combatant training outcomes through contemporary and fit for purpose target systems and Consumables, managed and sustained under the Program.

This Statement of Requirement (SOR) defines the requirement for the establishment of a Standing Offer for the supply of the Corrugated Target System Consumable products in support of Army training activities. This Corrugate Target System comprises of target board and decal products. The products to be supplied are used on Defence training ranges to enable the safe, realistic and effective conduct of live-fire weapons training. The products will be engaged with live ammunition and are expected to be replaced as a result of ballistic damage, weathering and normal range wear.

The Consumable Corrugated Target System must provide clear visual definition and consistent engagement characteristics, and must be suitable for use with the weapon systems and ammunition types where specified in this tender. As Consumables, they are required to be cost-effective, available in relevant volumes and supplied to support sustained and surge training demand.

To the east is the capital city Brisbane, and to the west are the rural and agricultural areas of the Brisbane, Lockyer and Fassifern Valleys. The city is ideally positioned on the national road network - 40 minutes drive from Brisbane, an hours drive from the Gold Coast and 60 minutes drive from domestic and international air and sea ports.
Ipswich comprises an area of 1090 square kms and has a population of 180,000 people. Ipswich enjoys a subtropical climate and is a safe, friendly and multicultural city. Residents come from 115 different ethnic backgrounds, speaking 84 languages.
As Queensland's oldest provincial city, Ipswich has a rich history. It is renowned for its architectural, natural and cultural heritage. Ipswich proudly preserves and still operates from many of its historical buildings and homes, with more than 6000 heritage-listed sites. Ipswich also has a range of charming townships within the western rural areas of the city, each with its own legitimate claims of historical significance.

title: Palm Island Walking Trails & Tourism Activation Project - Design & Construct
description:
Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council (Council) is seeking a suitably qualified and experienced Design & Construct (D&C) Contractor to undertake the design and construction of the Palm Island Walking Trails & Tourism Activation Project.

The Project comprises the delivery of the walking trails, Cultural Welcome Precinct, eco accommodation / tourism accommodation base and associated tourism-supporting infrastructure described in Part B – Specification, including all investigations, surveys, assessments, design, approvals, construction, testing, commissioning, documentation and handover required to deliver the Works.

The procurement is an implementation procurement based on the Project outcomes and recommendations identified in Part B. Tenderers are required to demonstrate the capability, capacity and methodology necessary to deliver the Works within Palm Island's remote-island, cultural, environmental and logistical context and achieve Practical Completion by 31 December 2027.

Suitably qualified Tenderers with proven capability, capacity, and sound financial and technical background to deliver the Specification outlined in this Invitation to Tender are invited to participate in this Invitation to Tender process.

vendorPanelDetails.background:
The Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council is a local government area in Queensland, established to manage the Palm Island group and provide services to its community. The Council is a special local government area that was established under a Deed of Grant in Trust on 27 October 1986. The Council was previously known as the Palm Island Community Council, which had limited powers compared to its current governance structure.

The Council is responsible for local governance and community services including parks and gardens, roads, the library, cemeteries, waste management, animal and pest control, water and sewerage and the Palm Island Airport, and ensuring the needs of the Aboriginal community are met.

publicQuestions.question:
1. Question

Are subdivisions required/expected for the walking tracks, Cultural Welcome Precinct or Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base?

Background / Context

Does Council require the walking tracks, Cultural Welcome Precinct or Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base to be managed separately from the balance of the land/lots on which they are to be located, thereby requiring reconfiguration of a lot to establish separate title?

2. Question

Does Council consider the construction (operational works) of any section of the proposed walking track network to constitute assessable development under the Palm Island Planning Scheme 2016, noting that portions of the proposed alignment are located within flood prone land or land below 20 meters AHD?

Background / Context

Based on the preliminary walking track alignments shown in the Palm Island Track Network Report (Tricky Tracks, January 2026), sections which are expected to require heavy and moderate construction are indicatively:

* Proposed on land located below 20mAHD; and

* within land subject to flooding and/or prone to erosion as identified on overlay maps OM 1 to 4.2.   

Relevantly, under the Palm Island Planning Scheme 2016, operational works are impact assessable to the extent the works are within floodplain, erosion-prone or coastal hazard areas, or involve specified excavation and fill thresholds below 20m AHD.

3. Question

Does Council have better or more accurate overlay mapping (particularly floodplain and erosion-prone mapping) for the walking track alignments?

Background / Context

The planning scheme overlay mapping is not sufficiently detailed to confirm whether all sections of the proposed walking tracks are subject to flooding and/or erosion constraints.

4. Question

Does Council consider the walking tracks to be operational works under the Palm Island Planning Scheme 2016 and the Planning Act 2016, or are the walking tracks considered to be a material change of use (or both)?

Background / Context

The construction of a walking track is usually not a material change of use. Walking tracks are more commonly defined and assessed as operational works where construction involves earthworks, vegetation clearing or other physical alterations to land.

 The planning scheme definition of Environment Facility includes walking tracks as an example land use. Accordingly, does Council consider the establishment of the proposed walking tracks a material change of use for Environment Facility and operational works (or both)?

5. Question

Does Council agree that the land use for the Cultural Welcome Precinct is "Park"

Background / Context

Under the planning scheme land use definitions, a community use involves the use of premises for providing artistic, social or cultural facilities, or community services, to the public. The examples provided, namely an art gallery, community centre, community hall, library and museum, all share the common characteristic of being identifiable facilities used for the delivery of cultural, social or community functions.

However, while the Cultural Welcome Precinct incorporates cultural expression, interpretation and opportunities for gathering, its primary purpose is not considered to be the provision of a dedicated artistic, social or cultural facility or community service. Rather, it functions as an openly accessible public realm space that facilitates informal recreation, gathering, movement and cultural recognition. The precinct is not intended to operate as a gallery, museum, community centre, performance venue or other comparable facility through which cultural or community services are provided.

The embedded cultural features of the precinct are therefore ancillary to its broader role as park (as defined in the Palm Island Planning Scheme).

Accordingly, the land use is considered to be characterised as a “Park” than as premises used for providing artistic, social or cultural facilities or community services to the public, as contemplated by the definition of community use.

6. Question

Does Council agree that under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, the land use for the Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base is Nature-based tourism?

Background / Context

If so, the establishment of the Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base is code assessable development under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, within the Family Camp Precinct; otherwise, impact assessment may apply.

7. Question

In the event that any component of the project is determined to constitute assessable development under the Planning Act 2016 requiring a development permit (and assuming no referral agencies are involved), would Council be willing to consider issuing an exemption certificate under section 46 of the Planning Act 2016?

Background / Context

Council may issue an exemption certificate pursuant to (and subject to satisfying the requirements of) s46 of the Planning Act.

8. Question

Could Council advise whether it or the Minggamingga Rangers hold any existing flora, fauna or vegetation data for the island? 

Background / Context

Understanding this will help size the investigations allowance in Item 2 of the Pricing Schedule
publicQuestions.answer:
Answer to Question 1

Council does not currently require or expect separate lots or titles for the walking tracks, Cultural Welcome Precinct or Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base as part of the D&C scope.

The assets may remain within the existing land tenure arrangements. Any future lease, licence, concession or commercial operating arrangement will be considered separately by Council and will remain subject to applicable planning, land tenure, Native Title and ILUA requirements.

Answer to Question 2

The walking-track project includes operational work associated with the physical works; however, Council does not consider the Planning Scheme triggers for floodplain, erosion-prone areas or works below 20 m AHD to make that operational work assessable where the Schedule 6, section 8 public-sector-entity provision applies.

Separate State-level approvals may still apply depending on the final design and alignment, including for coastal, tidal, marine plant, vegetation or waterway matters.

Answer to Question 3

For coastal erosion, Council has more recent coastal-hazard information, including revised erosion-prone area mapping that reflects the protection provided by existing seawalls and reduces the mapped erosion hazard in parts of the township foreshore.

Council does not currently have equivalent refined flood/overland-flow modelling; further modelling has been recommended.

The July 2026 First Nations Coastal Hazard Study – Asset Exposure and Recommendations Final Report will be issued separately by addendum and will replace the previous version included in the procurement documentation.

Answer to Question 4

Both aspects are relevant.

The walking-track project includes an operational-work component associated with the physical works. As outlined in the response to Question 2, Council does not consider that component assessable solely because of the local Planning Scheme operational-work triggers where the Schedule 6 public-sector-entity provision applies.

Separately, the Planning Scheme expressly identifies walking tracks as an Environment facility. Council therefore considers establishment of the walking-track use to constitute a material change of use for an Environment facility, with the applicable assessment pathway determined by the relevant zones and overlays.

Answer to Question 5

Council considers the Cultural Welcome Precinct, as currently proposed, to be principally a Community use under the Planning Scheme.

The proposed cultural performance, interpretation, gallery, artist/maker, visitor orientation and community gathering functions align with that use, with associated amenities, catering and incidental sale of local art and cultural products treated as ancillary activities.

Answer to Question 6

Based on the currently proposed scope, Council's preliminary view is that Nature-based tourism is the most appropriate land-use classification for the Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base.

The Planning Scheme definition of Nature-based tourism expressly extends to tourist and visitor short-term accommodation intended to support appreciation of environmental, cultural or heritage values and identifies accommodation such as lodges, cabins, huts and tented camps as examples. This is closely aligned with the proposed low-impact eco-accommodation concept.

Answer to Question 7

Council does not propose to rely on an exemption certificate for the core MCU or overall project. The Walking Trails and Cultural Welcome Precinct comprise substantive new tourism and cultural development, including new trails, visitor facilities, an amphitheatre, cultural and artist spaces, gathering areas and associated infrastructure. Given the project scope, Council does not consider it appropriate to characterise the effects of the whole MCU as minor or inconsequential for the purposes of section 46.

Where operational work is already not assessable under the Schedule 6 public-sector provision, no exemption certificate would be required. Council may, however, consider a section 46 exemption certificate for discrete, low-impact works where the statutory criteria are satisfied.

Answer to Question 8

Council is not in a position to provide any additional site-specific flora, fauna or vegetation datasets beyond the information already included in the procurement documentation.

The Principal Contractor will be responsible for obtaining and verifying all environmental information required for detailed design, approvals and construction, including relevant desktop searches, field investigations and specialist flora/fauna/vegetation surveys. Tenderers should make appropriate allowance for these activities in their submissions.

publicQuestions.question:
Dear Tender Team,

We are seeking clarification regarding the Wharf/Foreshore Welcome Precinct and its interface with the separately tendered Cultural Walk construction works.

Could Council please confirm:

1 - Which buildings, shelters, toilets, showers, kitchen facilities and associated structures within the Wharf/Foreshore Welcome Precinct are required to be designed and constructed under this tender, as distinct from the Cultural Walk construction contract?

2 - Whether existing or proposed potable water, wastewater, electrical and stormwater infrastructure will be available to service these facilities, and whether relevant drawings, connection locations and capacity information can be provided.

3 - Whether the welcome precinct and elevated camping area are intended to contain separate amenities and kitchen facilities, or whether some facilities are shared.

4 - Whether Council will facilitate design coordination between the successful tenderers, GHD and relevant Council representatives during the pre-construction phase to align architectural treatments, colour selections, material finishes, landscape interfaces and utility servicing arrangements.

Our intention is to ensure that the two projects are complementary, that infrastructure responsibilities are clearly defined, and that our tender accurately reflects the required scope.

Kind regards.
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Wharf/Foreshore Welcome Precinct scope and interface with Cultural Walk

The WTRL01 D&C Contractor is responsible for designing and delivering the Welcome Precinct, including public toilets, shade, seating, water points, visitor orientation, Rangers welcome point, cultural gathering area, catering/community kitchen facilities, artist/display infrastructure and associated connections.

Final arrangements are subject to design development and Council approval, avoiding duplication with the separately delivered Cultural Walk.

The Cultural Walk includes pathways, shade structures, lighting, electrical infrastructure and cultural/public-realm works, but excludes permanent toilets, showers and kitchen facilities.

Showers are required only at the Eco-accommodation site.

2. Potable water, wastewater, electrical and stormwater servicing

Servicing arrangements are to be investigated, verified and developed by the WTRL01 D&C Contractor. Existing infrastructure capacity or connection availability should not be assumed.

Tenderers are responsible for investigating existing services and potential connection points during the site visit, with further verification and design development by the successful Contractor.

3. Amenities and kitchen facilities at both locations

Both locations require separate facilities:

Welcome Precinct: Public toilets and community kitchen/catering facilities.

Eco-accommodation: Guest toilets, showers, shared kitchen/catering and communal dining facilities, including appropriate water, wastewater, waste and energy solutions.

Final configurations are subject to design development and Council approval.

4. Design and interface coordination

Yes. Council will facilitate coordination between the WTRL01 Contractor, Cultural Walk contractor, and relevant stakeholders during design development.

Coordination will address physical interfaces, levels, pathways, materials, drainage, utilities, construction staging, wayfinding and cultural elements.

Each contractor remains responsible for its respective contractual scope. Any changes will be managed through the applicable contract.

publicQuestions.question:
Dear Tender Team,

Given that construction is due to commence in April, after the wet season, could the council confirm that we can be on the island to conduct community engagement and ecological assessments in Jan/Feb, even though it will be the wet season?

Will families/ communities be able to engage in the process at this time?
publicQuestions.answer:
Yes. Council anticipates that the successful Contractor may undertake site investigations, ecological assessments and Council-coordinated community/stakeholder engagement during January and February 2027, notwithstanding that this period falls within the wet season.

This is consistent with the current Project program, which provides for mobilisation from December 2026 and requires the key investigations, assessments, design and approvals necessary to enable construction to be progressed by 31 March 2027, ahead of the planned construction commencement in April 2027. The Contractor is required to allow for wet-season conditions, weather disruption and Palm Island access/logistics constraints in developing its program.

Council does not presently anticipate that the wet season would, of itself, prevent engagement with families, community members, Rangers or other relevant stakeholders during January/February. However, engagement will need to be planned and coordinated with Council, and the availability of particular individuals or groups cannot be guaranteed for specific dates. The Contractor should therefore allow sufficient flexibility in its engagement program.

Similarly, ecological fieldwork may be undertaken during this period where appropriate. The Contractor remains responsible for determining, through suitably qualified specialists, the scope, methodology and seasonal timing of ecological investigations necessary to support the design and approvals. The Specification expressly anticipates flora/fauna/ecology and other environmental investigations as part of the D&C scope.

All site activities will remain subject to weather and cyclone conditions, safe access, WHS requirements, cultural protocols and coordination with Council and relevant stakeholders. Community and cultural engagement is to be undertaken through the Council-led engagement process rather than independently by the Contractor.

publicQuestions.question:
Good morning,

Can Council please confirm the following

1. Council has confirmed a material change of use (MCU) is needed for the trails (Environment facility), the precinct (Community use) and the lodge (Nature-based tourism). Please confirm, for each: (a) who lodges the application (Council or the Contractor), (b) whether Council is the assessment manager, (c) whether it is code or impact assessable in its zone and precinct, and (d) whether Council application fees apply. We believe these items will directly impact the 31 March approvals milestone

2. An earlier RFI response mentioned that a Hazard Study would be issues by addendum. Can this document be provided?

3. Council notes that further flood and overland flow modelling has been recommended. Is that modelling expected in the Contractor’s scope? What flood immunity should the precinct buildings, the lodge and the trails be designed to?

4. For the welcome precinct, is the catering / community kitchen to be designed to commercial food premises standard, and who will operate it? Also, is there a minimum number of toilets, or a design basis such as ferry passenger numbers or event crowd size?

5. Can Council provide any existing survey, LiDAR or aerial survey, and as-constructed or GIS records for water, sewer, stormwater and electrical services near the precinct, town footpath and lodge site?

6. How many working days will Council take to review design submissions at each hold point?

7. Can the welcome precinct share the new electrical supply proposed for the Cultural Walk

8. Given the large number of outstanding items, and recent RFI responses, would Council be in a position to extend the submission date for this tender, to allow Contractors to compile these responses?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Development Applications – MCU Requirements

(a) Application responsibility

The successful Contractor, through appropriately qualified planning consultants, will be responsible for preparing, coordinating and lodging all required development applications, including supporting documentation and technical assessments, in accordance with the tender requirements.

Where applications require Council to act as the applicant or provide landowner consent, Council will facilitate the necessary authorisations. The Contractor remains responsible for coordinating the applications and associated approval processes.

(b) Assessment manager

Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council will ordinarily be the assessment manager for Material Change of Use (MCU) applications under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, except where otherwise prescribed by State legislation.

Council's statutory assessment responsibilities will remain separate from its role as Project Principal.

(c) Assessment category

For the purposes of tender preparation, it is assumed that the proposed infrastructure, including the walking trails, Cultural Welcome Precinct and eco-accommodation, will not be implemented within the Family Camp Precinct.

On this basis, the anticipated development assessment pathways are as follows:

Walking trails (Environment facility): Code assessment is provided for under the Environmental Management and Conservation Zone provisions, subject to the applicable conditions and confirmation of the final development footprint.

Cultural Welcome Precinct (Community use): Generally code assessable within the Major Centre Zone and Recreation and Open Space Zone, subject to confirmation of the applicable zoning and development characteristics.

Eco-accommodation (Nature-based tourism): The assessment category must be confirmed against the final location and relevant provisions of the Environmental Management and Conservation Zone, including the specific precinct-related conditions in Table 5.4.1. Impact assessment may be required.

The assumption that development will occur outside the Family Camp Precinct does not, by itself, establish that all components will be code assessable.

The Contractor remains responsible for verifying the relevant land-use classifications, zoning, overlays and statutory assessment requirements during design development.

(d) Application fees

Council's adopted 2026–2027 Fees and Charges Schedule identifies a fee of $590 (including GST) for an application for preliminary or development approval.

Tenderers should allow for applicable statutory application, assessment and certification fees unless otherwise formally advised by Council.

The Contractor must incorporate the necessary investigations, design and statutory approvals into the Project Program, having regard to the 31 March 2027 milestone.

Council notes that the milestone relates to the investigations, assessments, design and approvals necessary to enable construction commencement. Progressive approval and construction packages may be proposed where appropriate and legally permissible.

2. Hazard Study

Council acknowledges the previous advice regarding provision of the Coastal Hazard Study.

Council is arranging for the relevant study to be issued through a separate tender addendum, subject to confirmation of the latest available version.

The study is provided as reference information and does not replace the Contractor's responsibility for undertaking site-specific investigations, assessments and design verification.

3. Flood and Overland Flow Modelling

The successful Contractor is responsible for undertaking all necessary site-specific flood, drainage, hydrological and hydraulic investigations and modelling required to inform the design and obtain statutory approvals.

Council has not prescribed a single flood immunity level applicable to all Project components.

The Contractor must determine and justify appropriate flood immunity and resilience criteria for the Cultural Welcome Precinct, eco-accommodation and walking trails, having regard to the Palm Island Planning Scheme, applicable overlays, relevant design standards, statutory requirements, site-specific conditions and intended operational use.

For buildings, the design must address appropriate finished floor levels, stormwater management, flood resilience and safe access.

For walking trails, the design must consider seasonal inundation, overland flow, erosion, drainage, user safety and appropriate operational restrictions during severe weather events.

The proposed design criteria and supporting technical assessments are to be submitted for Council review during design development.

4. Cultural Welcome Precinct – Kitchen and Toilets

The catering/community kitchen is intended to support community activities, cultural events and visitor experiences.

The final operating arrangements have not yet been confirmed. For tender purposes, the facility should be designed to accommodate commercial food preparation and catering activities, including compliance with Food Safety Standard 3.2.3 and other applicable regulatory requirements.

Council is separately engaging a Tourism Commercial Development and Operational Readiness Partner to assist with developing the operating model. The ultimate operator will be determined by Council through this process.

Regarding toilets, Council has not prescribed a fixed number beyond applicable statutory requirements.

The Contractor must determine an appropriate amenities provision based on anticipated ferry passenger movements, walking trail visitors, community use, event attendance, accessibility requirements and relevant National Construction Code provisions.

The proposed design capacity, assumptions and functional arrangements are to be presented for Council review during design development.

5. Survey, LiDAR and Existing Services Information

Council does not presently have a comprehensive, verified package of topographical survey, LiDAR, as-constructed drawings or underground services records covering all proposed Project locations.

The successful Contractor remains responsible for completing the necessary surveys, investigations, services locating and verification activities, including confirmation of existing infrastructure locations, connection points and available capacities.

Tenderers should make appropriate allowances for these activities in accordance with the Specification.

6. Council Design Review Periods

For programming purposes, an indicative allowance of 5 working days is proposed for Council's review of complete and coordinated design submissions at formal design hold points.

Review periods may vary depending on submission complexity, specialist input, stakeholder consultation and other Project requirements.

The successful Contractor will be required to establish a Design Management Plan and coordinated submission schedule for agreement with Council.

Council will endeavour to facilitate progressive reviews and release of individual work packages where practicable to support the Project Program.

Statutory assessment periods, ILUA/native title processes, cultural heritage approvals and other external approval requirements are separate from this indicative design review allowance and must be estimated into the Contractor's Project Program.

7. Electrical Supply – Cultural Walk Interface

Council acknowledges the potential opportunity to share electrical infrastructure between the Cultural Welcome Precinct and the separately delivered Cultural Walk project.

However, shared electrical supply has not been confirmed, and the availability or capacity of the proposed Cultural Walk electrical infrastructure cannot presently be guaranteed.

The successful Contractor will be required to coordinate with Council and the Cultural Walk project team to investigate potential shared servicing arrangements, including electrical capacity, infrastructure requirements, timing, approvals, ownership and operational considerations.

For tender purposes, proponents should allow for a complete and compliant electrical servicing solution for the Cultural Welcome Precinct.

Any potential efficiencies through shared infrastructure may be identified as opportunities for consideration during design development.

8. Request for Tender Extension

Council acknowledges the matters raised and the associated tender preparation requirements.

Council has already extended the original tender closing date from 16 October to 30 October 2026.

Having considered the additional clarification requests and information being provided to tenderers, Council has decided to grant a further one-week extension.

The revised tender closing date will be Friday, 6 November 2026 at 2:00 pm AEST.

This extension will be formalised through an addendum issued to all tenderers via VendorPanel. All other tender requirements remain unchanged unless expressly amended.

Any additional information or formal amendments will be communicated to all tenderers through VendorPanel.

Tenderers remain responsible for submitting their proposals in accordance with the tender requirements, including identification of relevant assumptions, qualifications and proposed delivery methodologies.

publicQuestions.question:
Dear Council,

Under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, there is a probability that some aspects of the project may trigger the need for development approvals that are subject to impact assessment and, therefore, require public notification in accordance with the Planning Act 2016 and the Development Assessment Rules.

For development applications requiring public notification, the applicant must:

* Place a notice on the land.

* Publish a notice in the prescribed publication medium (historically a newspaper, although alternative arrangements may be available in certain circumstances).

* Give notice to adjoining landowners.

* Lodge evidence demonstrating compliance with the public notification requirements with the assessment manager.

While we acknowledge that, under Queensland's development assessment system, the applicant is responsible for undertaking public notification (rather than the local government), many regional and remote councils provide administrative assistance and recover the associated costs from the applicant. This assistance may include:

* Publishing details of development applications on the council's development application register or website.

* Erecting or arranging public notification signage on the subject land on behalf of the applicant.

* Providing guidance and templates to assist applicants in complying with the public notification requirements.

Notwithstanding the above, responsibility for ensuring compliance with the public notification requirements remains with the applicant.

Given the unique circumstances of Palm Island and the practical challenges associated with undertaking public notification in a remote community, we would appreciate Council's advice regarding the assistance it may provide in facilitating public notification.

In particular, could Council please advise whether it is able to assist with:

* publishing notices on Council's website or development application register;

* arranging or installing public notification signage;

* identifying appropriate publication methods for the locality;

* providing guidance on notification requirements specific to Palm Island; or

* any other administrative support typically provided to applicants undertaking public notification.

Understanding the level of assistance available will assist with project planning and help ensure that any future development applications can efficiently satisfy the statutory public notification requirements.

With thanks.
publicQuestions.answer:
Council acknowledges the practical challenges associated with public notification on Palm Island and confirms that reasonable administrative assistance may be provided, subject to availability and prior arrangements.

Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council is ordinarily the assessment manager for development applications under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, except where another assessment manager is prescribed under the Planning Regulation 2017.

In response to the specific enquiries:

Website publication: Council can facilitate publication of development application notices on its website, subject to the applicable statutory requirements and provision of the necessary documentation. Council currently publishes development application notices through its website.

Public notification signage: The successful Contractor will be responsible for preparing, installing and maintaining the required signage as part of the development approval process. Council may assist with local coordination and practical arrangements, subject to availability and prior agreement.

Publication methods: Council, as the anticipated assessment manager, will identify the applicable public notification requirements through the statutory development assessment process, including the confirmation notice where required. Depending on the applicable requirements, publication may be undertaken through a newspaper and Council's website. Council can also provide guidance on suitable supplementary local communication channels.

Local planning requirements: Council can provide general guidance on the Palm Island Planning Scheme, applicable public notification procedures and relevant local considerations. The successful Contractor remains responsible for obtaining appropriate professional planning advice and coordinating the necessary development approvals.

Additional administrative support: Council will consider reasonable requests for assistance with local logistics, coordination and community communication on a case-by-case basis, subject to resource availability and agreement on any associated costs.

The successful Contractor remains responsible under the tender requirements for identifying, managing and coordinating all necessary development approvals and associated public notification activities. Statutory responsibilities for public notification remain with the applicant, in accordance with the Planning Act 2016 and Development Assessment Rules.

Council notes that the requirement for impact assessment and public notification will depend on the final proposed design, development classification and applicable planning provisions.

Any administrative assistance provided by Council will be separate from its statutory responsibilities as assessment manager and will not constitute an indication of development approval.

publicQuestions.question:
Dear Council,

Following discussions with our engineering and certification consultant, we respectfully request a two-week extension to the closing date for the Palm Island Walking Trails & Tourism Activation Project – Design & Construct tender.

Our consultant has requested additional time to assess the engineering, investigation and certification requirements associated with the Welcome Precinct, particularly given the current uncertainty surrounding the availability of essential site information.

We recognise that some of this information may not currently be available within Council's records. However, we also understand that relevant investigations and surveys may be undertaken or become available through other projects being delivered concurrently within the precinct.

In particular, we seek clarification regarding the availability, or anticipated timing, of the following:

* Geotechnical investigations and reports relevant to proposed structures and foundations.

* Existing services and utilities mapping, including water, wastewater, electrical and stormwater infrastructure, together with available connection points and capacities.

* Topographical survey information, including surveyed Reduced Levels (RLs), site contours and relevant datum information for the Welcome Precinct.

We respectfully request that Council consider providing an indicative timeline for when this information may become available to the successful contractor, including whether any investigations are anticipated to be undertaken as part of the concurrent Cultural Walk works.

The requested extension would allow our engineering and certification consultant sufficient time to assess the outstanding requirements, identify necessary allowances and provide more reliable advice on the anticipated costs, approvals and delivery timeframes.

We believe this would assist tenderers in preparing more accurate and commercially responsible submissions, while reducing the potential for significant variations, unforeseen investigation costs and program delays during delivery.

We appreciate Council's consideration of this request and look forward to your response.

Kind regards

publicQuestions.question:
1. Does Council remove or manage contamination levels in FOGO and GO before it is transported to the final processing facility?

2. What level of contamination (i.e. 2% by mass) does Council consider to be deemed as "ordinary contamination".

3. Does Council have any specified days that it would like to deliver FOGO and GO?

4. What definition or classification does Council use for Processed product? e.g. does it need to meet AS4454 criteria or other specification?
publicQuestions.answer:
Q1. Does Council remove or manage contamination levels in FOGO and GO before it is transported to the final processing facility?

A1. No. Council does not undertake pre-processing or contamination removal of FOGO or GO prior to delivery to the processing facility. Material is delivered as collected, and the Service Provider is responsible for monitoring contamination levels, managing contamination, processing the material, and disposing of any contamination or residual waste in accordance with the Contract requirements.

Council's waste collection contractor does, however, undertake a fortnightly bin audit program. During these audits, staff visually inspect up to 60 FOGO bins per fortnight for contamination. Where contamination is estimated to exceed 10% of the bin contents, the bin is not collected, and educational material is provided to the resident. Where contamination is estimated to be less than 10% of a bins content, the bin is collected and tagged with an educational notice identifying the incorrect materials observed.

________________________________________

Q2. What level of contamination (i.e. 2% by mass) does Council consider to be deemed as "ordinary contamination"?

A2. Council has not prescribed a specific contamination threshold or percentage for ordinary contamination. Tenderers are required to propose contamination thresholds, measurement methodologies, and management procedures as part of their tender submission for Council's review and approval. Ordinary contamination is expected to be managed by the Service Provider as part of the contracted processing services. Prohibited or hazardous waste is treated separately under the Contract. For information, Council's household organics bin audit undertaken by Ann Price Consulting in May 2026 estimated the average contamination rate within Ballina Shire household organic bins to be approximately 3.9%. This figure is provided as historical performance information only and is not intended to represent a contractual contamination threshold.

________________________________________

Q3. Does Council have any specified days that it would like to deliver FOGO and GO?

A3. Council has not specified particular delivery days for FOGO or GO deliveries. However, the RFT requires the processing facility to be available to receive Delivered Material during the minimum operating hours specified in the tender documentation.

For information, Council aims to collect and deliver a relatively consistent quantity of material across each weekday to support the efficient operation of its collection services and transport resources. Tenderers should therefore anticipate regular weekday deliveries, with delivery volumes generally distributed as evenly as practicable throughout the week.

The minimum receival hours specified in the RFT are:

•	Monday to Friday: 7:00am to 3:30pm

•	Weekends and Public Holidays: 9:00am to 2:00pm

Council's expectation is that the facility will be capable of accepting Delivered Material during these times.

________________________________________

Q4. What definition or classification does Council use for Processed Product? For example, does it need to meet AS4454 criteria or another specification?

A4. Processed Product is defined as any product recovered from or produced using the Delivered Material during the provision of the Services. Processed Product must comply with AS 4454-2012 Compost, Soil Conditioners and Mulches where applicable. The Service Provider must also comply with all relevant NSW EPA requirements, including any applicable Resource Recovery Orders, Exemptions, and the Compost Order in force at the time.

** ABOUT THE BEGA VALLEY **

The Bega Valley Shire is located at the south-eastern corner of New South Wales, halfway between Australia’s two largest cities, Sydney and Melbourne and three hours’ drive from the nation’s capital, Canberra.

Our coastal fringe extends from Wallaga Lake in the north to Cape Howe and the Victorian border in the south. Collectively this 225-kilometre section forms the beautiful Sapphire Coast, the heart of Australia’s Coastal Wilderness.

Our community vision explains our collective aspiration that we are an inclusive and welcoming community that integrates quality of life, prosperity, sustainable development and conservation of the environment. Our connection to Country is guided by the culture and heritage of our Traditional Owners.

** ABOUT COUNCIL **

Bega Valley Shire Council is responsible for providing all of the typical local government services across the Bega Valley Shire including maintaining a broad range of assets valued at over $1.7 billion that allow our visitors and community alike to live, work and play.

The Bega Valley Shire is governed by an elected Council comprising nine Councillors. Councillors provide leadership and establish policy and strategic direction for the organisation and the future of the shire.

Delivering the day to day services for council is a professional and dynamic staff cohort of over 560 people including full time, contract and casual positions.

Contractors to council play an important and valued role, assisting us delivering services and projects to the highest of standards and value for money.

** WHAT COUNCIL DOES **

Provide and maintain community facilities such as:
•	Parks and sportsgrounds
•	Playgrounds and skate parks
•	Sapphire Aquatic centre Pambula and swimming pools throughout the shire
•	Sports and recreation facilities throughout the Shire
•	Local libraries in Bega, Bermagui, Eden and Merimbula
•	Preschools and Childcare centres in Bega and Eden, and our Mobile service for Candelo and Bemboka
•	Merimbula Airport, Bega Saleyards and Cemeteries throughout the Shire

We care for the environment by:
•	Managing and enhancing bushland areas
•	Providing environmental and waste education and recycling services
•	Responding to pollution incidents and prosecuting polluters
•	Monitoring the water quality of the Shire’s estuaries
•	Planting trees and controlling noxious weeds
•	Beneficially recycling and reusing treated effluent

We create a safer place to live by:
•	Maintaining and improving roads, footpaths and stormwater drains
•	Working with emergency organisations such as the Rural Fire Service, State Emergency Service, NSW Police and NSW Surf Life Saving
•	Managing the keeping of companion animals
•	Inspecting food premises
•	Treating and supplying drinking water to our community
•	Treating sewage to a high standard to protect human health

We enhance our community by:
•	Listening to community views
•	Holding citizenship ceremonies, Australia Day Celebrations and the Seniors week luncheon known as the Golden Gig
•	Offering services for seniors, young people, new migrants and people with a disability
•	Providing grants to community organisations
•	Supporting local community groups such as sporting clubs, arts, migrant groups and charities
•	Encouraging and promoting volunteering in our communities

We plan for the future by:
•	Planning and managing the urban environment
•	Preserving heritage sites
•	Consulting with the community about its needs
•	Developing long term strategic plans for Council and the Shire
